data.title: Online Peer Training
data.description: COVID19 -We want to ensure that, in moving our current peer training online, women with learning disabilities and/or autism can still access training and support to disclose ongoing or historic abuse, and that these disclosures will be handled sensitively and efficiently.In doing so we will be developing the skills of our peer education team and empowering them as online trainers; ensuring peer education can continue in the best way currently available. ?Us Too? peer educators are enthusiastic about developing online learning, but have told us that they lack the expertise and resources to do this.Owing to the current crisis, we need to adapt our training for online delivery in a way that is both effective and safe for women with learning disabilities and/or autism, continuing to keep them safe from domestic abuse. However, moving our training online poses significant challenges. Our peer training to date has often resulted in disclosures of abuse. It is critical that online training can be offered in a way that does not suppress disclosures, and ensures that learners are supported by staff who are trained and competent in enabling learning and processing disclosures when necessary. In face-to-face training situations the training team is skilled in giving permission for disclosures, offering immediate support, processing disclosures and following up. Our concern is that, in moving our training online, we would be delegating this task and responsibility to care staff who may lack the skill set to manage disclosures. We want to:- Consult with the project peer education team to ensure that project developments are guided by women with learned experience and will meet the needs of girls/women with learning disabilities and/or autism.- Work with a research partner (RIPFA: researchinpractice.org.uk)who will explore the issues and make recommendations for positive training delivery that keeps women safe and supports disclosure as we move to online delivery.- In partnership with RIPFA, develop protocols for social care organisations and carers on how to support women completing online training on sensitive issues.- Provide the technology that will enable the peer trainers to deliver their training online (latops/tablets, wifi access, licensing for a training platform.- Upskill the peer trainers to use this technology professionally and safely, so that they do not endanger themselves.- Provide external supervision for the training team from an expert counsellor.- Train 24 social care staff to support women with learning disabilities/autism undertake domestic abuse training.- Pilot an online domestic abuse workshop with women with learning disabilities/autism. - Gather the learning, and disseminate the protocols and learning materials free of charge throughout our networks.In doing this we will be meeting the stated funding criteria of working with a vulnerable group and meeting an unmet need.

data.title: Safe routes out of asylum destitution in Greater Manchester
data.description:
COVID19 -We would use this funding for our core work of providing safe accommodation and holistic support to our client group at this time. We are currently accommodating and supporting over 80 individuals across our 21 shared houses and in temporary placements in guesthouses. Providing this safe accommodation offers our clients an essential foundation to move out of hidden or street homelessness, and to access the support they need. 
 
 Our package of holistic support is tailored to the needs of each client, which we are continuing to deliver remotely and while practicing safe social distancing. Clients have regular catch up with our support workers who provide emotional support, offering empathy and encouragement, and support is offered on an ad-hoc basis when needed too. This could be help with accessing healthcare support, support to engage with exercising outside safely, or help with progressing a fresh asylum claim or a universal credit claim. The trusting relationships that our client support team have developed with our clients are more important than ever in these circumstances. 
 
 We are continuing to also support clients to take actions that will bring about a long term resolution to their homeless situations. For those seeking asylum, we continue to support people to progress asylum claims. For those with refugee status, we are supporting people to take steps towards safe, happy and fulfilling settlement in the UK. 
 
 We are also involved in efforts to encourage, coordinate and deliver accommodation and support for our client group at both local and national levels. Locally we are heavily involved in a variety of partnerships including the Greater Manchester Homelessness Network, through which we are helping to coordinate the distribution of donations. On a national level we are working with the NACCOM network, Refugee Action and others to advocate for our clients and look at solutions to specific challenges they are faced with at this time. 
 
 We would also like to take this opportunity to thank you for your support of our work ? we really appreciate it, and we are grateful for this opportunity to access further support at this time.

data.title: Croydon Voluntary Action Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 -We are seeking funding to support refugees and asylum seekers (RASs), specifically those who are newly arrived and living in temporary hostels in Croydon. Over the last couple of months CVA has been working to ensure that the most vulnerable people in Croydon receive basic necessities of food and medicines. However, as we progress to addressing additional needs relating to physical and mental health, stress and isolation we are seeking funding to ensure that RASs are not excluded. Currently RASs do not possess basic items of clothing to participate in outdoor exercise, especially to moderate levels of activity which result in sweating in order to contribute to improved physical health. Those that are confined to their room can do some exercise, but this would be enhanced with basic equipment, information and guidance on how to exercise safely and effectively. To enable them to participate in online activities they require tablets or smartphones - and data packages as hostels do not have WiFi and RASs can no longer access free WiFi through college, libraries or coffee shops. We will engage local sports partners to adapt online activities specifically for RASs and include additional opportunities to chat and socialise virtually and connect with the wider community.To further support RASs who are extremely isolated, we would like to offer a helpline staffed by volunteers who speak various community languages. Volunteers can offer health advice, information on expected behaviours and reassurance about safe exit from lockdown, currently causing great stress. We currently have over 400 volunteers registered with us but require support to manage and train volunteers and extend the existing helpline currently overwhelmed with emergency request to focus on this additional support. Once, lockdown starts to be relaxed, we want to offer exercise opportunities in pairs or small numbers (as allowed), with professional coaches offering support and ensuring that rules around social distancing and safety are incorporated.

data.title: Jewish Women's Aid Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -Due to the Coronavirus we have seen a marked increase in women seeking JWA?s support due to the domestic abuse they are experiencing. Whilst lockdown is a well- intentioned measure, we, and the rest of our sector are seeing it being misused to perpetrate escalating abuse on women ? this has been widely reported in the media. 
 - The number of women we supported this April increased by 27% compared with the last 3 years
 In April we delivered 25% more hours in direct client work than in March 
 JWA staff are all now working from home. This is exceptionally challenging as our caseworkers continue to prioritise the welfare of our service users, and we have had to invest in IT and office equipment such as laptops, printers, remote server capacity and IT support. 
 Because of this our office manager has been redeployed to manage IT support, telecomms, purchase of equipment and day-to-day troubleshooting across the organisation. Without her, meetings, supervisions, casework and board level interactions would not happen and JWA is reliant on her each day. She is funded from our core income which is now unsustainable and we are not certain what income will look like in the coming months and years.
 We are therefore applying for funding for part of her salary.

data.title: Early years support project
data.description: COVID19 -Our key focus currently is to provide reassurance, practical advice and emotional support to families who have a child or young person with a learning disability and to support the children with a range of activities that they can do at home. In the main, we are offering this support to families who currently use Leeds Mencap services however we are seeing an increased demand for this family support work. We are currently in contact with 143 families across the organisation who need our support however we have not yet reached out to all families who attend our holiday play schemes. The level of family support that we are offering each family has significantly increased as usually we would see families once a week but at present we are providing more intense phone support to many of the families. Please note that the above work also includes 24 families that are currently funded by Comic Relief through the Early Years Support Project.We have received 5 new referrals for Family Support over the last week. Our overall aim is to keep in touch with all our families and be there just to listen if need be. Keeping in touch helps us to identify early if more specialist help is needed eg behavioural support for the child/young person or deteriorating mental health in the parents.We are requesting additional funding to continue and expand this critical support over the next 6 months as follows:For parents/carersWe know that parents/carers of children and young people with a learning disability are under greater pressure during lock down and more serious social distancing measures as their children often need to be shielded or protected more due to underlying health conditions, their child?s behaviour and emotional well being may be more severely affected as they heavily rely on specialist support at school and the routine, they have greater support needs in relation to being kept busy. Respite services for families are not running and so the breaks parents and wider families rely on are not there. We are seeing this take its toll on the families we are supporting and aware that we need to keep in close contact to be able to spot when a family needs more support from us or needs more specialist help.In order to do this more effectively and meet the increased demand we need - to be able to keep in touch more frequently by phone, email and extend this to one to one video calls and later if within guidelines, offer one to one sessions- to facilitate the opportunity to meet up and socialise remotely eg. via zoom. - To be able to provide support for some common concerns and anxieties eg. cyberbullying, self-care, preparing for transition back to school which we?d like to offer through webinars/group sessions remotely.In order to do this we need to increase the hours of our existing family support worker and divert the focus of our Activities Coordinator and Family Services Manager to support this work.We are also requesting some funds for laptops to enable our Family Support staff to provide face to face virtual support (as detailed below) from home and in the office as our office computers do not have cameras and for some resources/equipment to support our older children/young people with disabilities. For children/young peopleAs lock down continues and the prospect of children with learning disabilities being able to return to school and normal activities soon, we are getting feedback from families - that the children are really missing their friends and want more social interaction- that it is becoming increasingly challenging to keep them occupied and for some their skills and learning are being affected - that this is resulting in increased challenging behaviour- that they are concerned the transition back to activities will be difficult as they will have lost the bonds they have made with friends and staffWe have been providing support for the children and young people via online activity packs and ideas, tailoring these to the needs of the particular children. As it is likely we won?t be able to run group activities until after the summer we want to increase and build on the activities we are providing by:- Organising virtual activity sessions for children and young people eg. Online bingo, ?chomp and chat? sessions (bring your favourite snack and chat to your friends) - Putting together and delivering to each child/young person (using social distancing guidelines) physical resource and activity packs. For example, next week, we are sending out a sensory pack for the younger children which include everything the families will need to make scented playdough. We don?t currently have materials to provide resource/activity packs for the older children in our clubs (7-18) and the young adults who attend our Friday club (18-25)- Arrange individual video calls with children/young people over the summer and in the run up to activities restarting to help them to maintain their bond with staff and for staff to be able to tailor support to them and support a smoother transition back when that happens.- Offer some one to one sessions for some of our young children with disabilities (0-3) who attend our playroom so we can offer specific tailored support and help them move onto the next step. This could be done by zoom or one to one face to face at a social distance (when guidelines allow). At the moment, we are anticipating that our face to face activities might resume in September but social distancing measures will mean that groups will be smaller so we anticipate that our online offering will need to continue alongside any face to face offerings. This funding would support the following outcomes: providing social opportunities for the children and parents so improving mental health and well being; retaining the relationships between the children within their groups and also with staff therefore supporting smooth return transitions and activity and resource packs will help to occupy the children and reduce challenging behaviour.

data.title: Virtual Hub
data.description:
COVID19 -We are requesting funding to develop a ?Virtual Support Hub? for young people who are participants on the Sports Horizon programme (funded by Comic Relief) and the AIMS mentoring project which is also based in the Young Person?s Hub. The AIMS project works with care leavers, young parents and in partnership with the Violence Reduction Partnership. 
 Young people supported by Sports Horizons have benefited from being able to access the physical ?Young Person?s Hub? where support is available all in one place ? access to mentors, skills courses, free wifi, breakfast clubs, specialist agency surgeries and enrichment activities. We want to replicate the benefits of the physical hub into a Virtual Hub:
 The Virtual Hub will offer:
 - Online chat with a mentor who will be available in the virtual Hub at set times during the day for example 2-4- for any ad hoc support/conversation - via online chat, any young person can access this. 
 - A menu of group activities each week that people can engage with including enrichment activities like mindfulness and group workshops on topics like CV writing.
 - Online chat with specialist agency who are offering drop in support at a certain time -Eg. mental health and substance misuse agencies who usually offer this support at the Hub.
 - One-to one video conversations with their mentor.
 - Delivery of AIMS Skills programmes which young people will be able to complete virtually.
 - Skills development videos including meals to cook.
 - Access to up to date information and resources 
 - The opportunity to interact with other young people via a message board, competitions, etc.
 Young People who are already disadvantaged are facing a difficult immediate future. The economic effects of the Coronavirus are going to cause significant unemployment and a depressed jobs market. This means that those who are currently furthest from employment are going to face even tougher barriers. 
 Having a Virtual Hub will increase the amount and quality of support we can provide while social distancing is in place; boost mental health and wellbeing for young people, reduce isolation and loneliness and ensure that young people do not miss out on opportunities to develop their skills and engage with life-changing support during this crisis. 
 We anticipate that even as lockdown measures are lifted, it will be a significant amount of time before the young people we are working with can engage with a pre-covid-19 level of structure and support in their lives. This Hub will help ensure that they do not face further disadvantage due to this crisis. 
 We have spoken to Olly Dawson, our Partnership manager at Comic Relief about this need and he has been positive about the way it would help us to support the young people we are working with. 
 We have been scoping out how a Hub could work with a couple of digital partners we already work with and have just secured funding for a Virtual Hub for our homeless services in Wales. We will use funding from Comic Relief to create a bespoke Hub (Using our Wales Hub as a template ? reducing cost) for young people who we support across Liverpool City Region; develop content, and digitilise some of our training skills programmes. We will also use for staff training, hosting and maintenance costs of the Hub for the first 6 months.
 Long-term, having an online Hub will also help us to reach groups who cannot access face to face support due to living in rural areas, their employment, family commitments, caring responsibilities or health situation. This will extend the reach of the support that we can provide ? giving this funding a significant legacy.

data.title: Elizabeth Foundation Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 -Funding will support indicative budget costs for the delivery of our national, online education and welfare programme, ?Lets Listen and Talk?. The programme reaches out across the UK to vulnerable deaf children aged 0 -5, their parents/carers and other professionals. It is now delivered free to all subscribers. ?Let?s Listen and Talk? is designed to provide practical help to parents who are concerned about their young deaf child. The programme focuses on development of vital speech, language and communication skills in the first five years of life, helping vulnerable children to develop and thrive in terms of their education, social inclusion and mental well-being. For many families, accessing essential learning support for a child who is hearing-impaired, deaf or who has delayed communication is challenging at the best of times (with an evidenced, significant lack of appropriate specialist support across the UK). As a result of the impact of COVID19/government lockdown restrictions, families and children with Special Educational Needs need our help ever more ? to support their learning, their well-being and their safety. Let?s Listen and Talk consists of targeted, online lessons (baby, toddler and preschool), with additional specialist papers around hearing assessment, technology, communication, cognitive skills, literacy, behaviour management and mental well-being. The programme can be accessed safely, whenever/wherever needed, using computers, tablets, smartphones. All families with deaf and hearing-impaired children are welcomed to the programme, regardless of faith, culture, economic or family background. In addition to written materials, families access secure, online videos to accompany each lesson. These are incredibly useful to parents, whether developing their skills & confidence to ?teach? or in need of extra visual support (i.e. for those with poor literacy skills, English as a second language, or those who are deaf themselves). Importantly parents have regular access to our expert staff via skype, email, telephone, zoom etc. Our team are there to answer questions, celebrate achievements, address areas of concern, maintain safeguarding protocols and sight families to other sources of support (for example if they are living in poverty). In March 2020, in order to meet the needs of the most vulnerable at this particularly difficult time, we decided to deliver the programme at no cost to families & external professionals, including local authority Teachers/staff at other nursery settings who are struggling. By helping to extend professionals knowledge and skills as well as parents, we are growing our reach and impact across the whole country, & building on the evidence we can share with wider audiences around the need for, and impact of specialist intervention for deaf children.Since the end of March, we have had over 480 additional subscribers to the programme and its growing daily. Your grant would help meet the cost of staff essential to the running and development of the programme.

data.title: YMCA East Surrey Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 - We want to continue to run WAVES online for young people already engaging with the project and for young people who are new to WAVES having been referred to us due to their mental health and wellbeing becoming worse under the lock down and COVID19. Since we started WAVES online we have had 16 new young people joining WAVES/being referred to us and 4 other organisations reaching out for support materials from WAVES.
 - We also want to support families who would access WAVES Meet and Eat.
 - What we would really like to do is to create and send out wellbeing self-care home kits for young people. In the absence of face to face WAVES sessions and other support for young people at this time we would like to develop and send out wellbeing self-care kits to promote wellbeing and help them to look after themselves. These kits would include, positive mental activities, materials to complete these activities, fun engaging worksheets, information about emergency support and other wellbeing items. We would involve young people in deciding and thinking about what they would benefit from in these kits. These will also act as a contact between WAVES and young people who are unable to take part in the online content every day. Lots of young people have expressed that money for them and their family is an issue right now and they are unable to afford things to keep them occupied and engage in activities other young people are able to do. These kits can also be adaptable for particular young people and families we work with. 
 - We would also use this money to start preparing for when we come out of lock down so we can continue WAVES as safely and successfully as possible, reducing stress and anxiety for young people. This would include investing in social distancing equipment, cleaning products and other protective equipment for members and staff.
 - In addition we want to provide 1-2-1 support for young people and families online to support them with the mental health and wellbeing difficulties they are facing. We want to provide an extra 3 hours of staff time every day of the week to support these families and young people and provide that support that can be responsive to changing needs.

data.title: Yorkshire Sport Foundation Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -The funding is required to support the most vulnerable families within two communities in Yorkshire, to improve their physical and mental health.
 Many families are experiencing hardship during this time, and do not have the access, support or knowledge as to how to look after their physical and mental health.
 We require funds to purchase family activity packs, which will provide equipment, information, advice and guidance to enable families to be active during this time.
 Activity packs will provide the vital, basic equipment to enable families to be active at home, or safely within their community, with their household. Simple messages and activity ideas will accompany the equipment, allowing all members of the family to get active. We will work with local community organisations and leaders to aid with translation and distribution of these packs.

data.title: Youth Action Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 -YouthAction?s Rainbow Factory based in the centre Belfast is a highly regarded school of performing arts and ?a beacon of light? for young people. It is unique as all its activities are underpinned by the very best youth work principles: -- It enables young people of all abilities and primarily from areas of social deprivation to improve their lives in a positive, vibrant way, through access to a dynamic range of high quality youth arts opportunities.- Especially working with those young people who are ?hard to reach?, marginalised, vulnerable, experiencing social/economic disadvantage, at risk of social exclusion or who would otherwise not have had the opportunity to explore their creativity or attend the arts. Many have little or no academic achievement or are underachievers at school. - In particular, we engage with young people who live with challenging conditions such as; depression, autism, Asperger?s syndrome, diabetes, physical disabilities, learning disabilities, mental health issues including social anxiety, self-harm and suicidal tendencies. - 70% of participants on current programmes reside in the top 25% of disadvantaged wards in N.I. 36% with a physical/mental impairment; 11% from ethnic minorities and 15% LGBT community.?It is a safe space to me, full of wonderful trusting people. It has brought me out of my shell and made me feel genuinely excited about life, for the first time ever. Here I have learnt how to battle my demons, look after myself in difficult times and how to be more confident in myself and my abilities. I believe that this group has saved my life. Thank you!??It was Rainbow Factory who helped me through a dark time and helped make me the young woman I am today.? During this time of unprecedented social isolation and anxiety, it is essential we quickly and professionally changed the methods we use so we can continue to support and engage the young people we work with. We did this by developing a new, free interactive performing arts site ?Virtual Rainbow Factory?: -- The site enables young people to participate in a diverse range of performing arts training and activities (we have completed 648 live Zoom ½ hr session) where young people can learn new creative skills and ignite old and new friendships.- We are offer new activities including: the ?UNLUGGED? area ? a platform where young people can ?perform? in whatever genre they like (poetry, music, art, voicing opinions, moviemaking etc.) to a wide and new audience. - Another area ?Spotlight on Your Mind? has a range of activities to help develop a positive emotion wellbeing including - a fun, safe live chat space where young people can be fully immersed in a daily flow activity. It will give them a much needed break from any negative energy and emotions as they focus on only this. - Young people are involved in the many fun and developmental elements of the site. Feedback from some of the young participants: - ?For me this is a life line. I?ve missed my Rainbow family more than anything!? ?I have days when I can?t leave my bed but if I make it to the online sessions I know that?s a small win and the day could get better.??I would be a lot sadder without this, here I can talk to people - I don?t talk to anyone else all week.? ?You've found new creative ways to keep us entertained and having a laugh - it?s the only time I use my brain!!?It make me less lonely and gives me something to do.??Not every place offers opportunities - when you?re having a bad day, you learn from it and make really good friends.?Since the Covid 19 crisis, we have been experiencing an increased demand to provide support to new young people. With support from Comic Relief we can develop and expand our Virtual Rainbow Factory to meet the critical needs of vulnerable young people right across Northern Ireland by: -- Engaging and supporting new young people who live in rural and urban areas.- Using our existing networks and membership groups across Northern Ireland to engage those most vulnerable, disadvantaged, marginalised young people and at risk of social exclusion, to reach out to those young people who for example: have low confidence/self-esteem; are mothers/carers; homeless; identify as other than heterosexual; offenders/at risk of offending; live with drug/ alcohol issues; have mental health issues or isolated from services.- Utilise our Spectrum model of work promoting inter-cultural dialogue to engage young people from ethnic minority backgrounds.- Expand our Connections programme which is delivered to young people with disabilities to those living in urban and rural areas. - Utilise 3 BME tutors and our partnerships with BME groups (such as, North West Islamic Association; Migrant Centre NI; Chinese Mandarin Speaker Association; Polish Language, Culture and Affairs) to ensure that young people from these communities participate.?Young people are at the heart of everything we do. Staying positive and having fun through the magical medium of the arts, is more important now than ever. Sometimes it?s good to remember that? no matter the storm just look for the Rainbow and it will always be there for you.? Maire Campbell, Artistic Director, YouthAction NI?s Rainbow Factory School of Performing Arts.

data.title: The Birmingham Settlement Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 -We are requesting funding towards our Birmingham Training Unit to help us deliver targeted mental health and mindfulness support and awareness to the communities where we work ? we have seen a significant rise in demand for help and we need to respond. As part of the Birmingham Children?s Partnership the Settlement has recently taken on the role of Voluntary Sector Lead for the Ladywood Constituency; the Partnership supports vulnerable children and families and includes statutory and community groups; it was in the planning for some time but has been brought forward as a direct result of Covid-19. We are also the lead agency for a similar Neighbourhood Network Scheme for Ladywood targeting older adults and linking direct with social work teams across the constituency. In addition to these examples, we also run our own programmes supporting individuals and families in the communities across the city where we work. Through these offers and the engagement we have maintained with our existing service users since lockdown measures were put in place, we have seen a marked rise in mental health problems including increased anxiety and stress, but we have also seen a decline in the level of support available at a local level. We know families are under increased pressure and face uncertainty moving forwards; many have little to do and social isolation is heightened for these already excluded communities. We have also seen a significant increase in the demand for debt and benefit advice through our existing money advice team which further adds to stress and tension for the individual and within the family unit. We can respond to this growing and unmet need through our Birmingham Training Unit?s ?Mental Health and Mindfulness? programme. In normal circumstances the Training Unit runs a mix of ?professional? courses for which we charge e.g. money advice to frontline staff, right to reside and similar; plus a range of ?soft? courses targeting communities and service users which are usually funded through trusts, foundations, and of course by re-investing fees from the ?professional? courses. However, since lockdown, and certainly for the medium term we have had to cease face-to-face and fee paying courses and our Trainer who is qualified to deliver mental health, mindfulness and similar workshops and support has been placed on furlough as the post is unfunded and we are unable to generate income to cover costs. A grant from Comic Relief would allow us to adapt and build the service relevant to the ?now? to be delivered online, utilising platforms such as ?Zoom?. The programme will be accessible for our current service users including young people, families, over 50s and those accessing our money advice services as well as the wider community as we promote the workshops through the programmes mentioned above. We will deliver the programme through:- Mindfulness sessions focusing on different practical mindfulness techniques, enabling people to take a step back from life?s pressures, practice methods for supporting their mental health and learn how to put crisis? into context with a view from a clear perspective. - Stress management sessions enabling people to understand the physiological effects of stress on their body and learn/practice techniques to cope with stress- Issue-based interactive workshops surrounding issues/debates relating to mental health- Mental Health Awareness training enabling people to recognise a mental health ?crisis?, to develop appropriate coping mechanisms and respond and take steps to positively enhance their mental wellbeing- Topic based training sessions covering ?Homelessness?, ?Drug Awareness, ?Safeguarding? to raise awareness of specific issues relating to mental health and the impact these can have on people?s lives, their friends and familyOur ?Mindfulness? training programme will complement our wider community action work where we are already now delivering a range of telephone/digital wellbeing services so enabling us to deliver a fuller Community Action and Training programme to those experiencing and susceptible to mental health issues during the coronavirus pandemic and beyond.We would specifically use the grant for: - Trainer @ 1.00 FTE incl. pension and NI for 6 months - Business Services Officer @ 0.4 FTE incl. pension and NI for 6 months to support the development of the programme and take us through Open College Network accreditation which will allow us to develop our programme meaning that service users will be able to gain a meaningful qualification to support their own personal and professional development.- Contribution to core costs (IT, finance, management etc) @ 23% of staff costs

data.title: Vintage Vibes Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 -This funding request is to help us quickly and creatively adapt our work, allowing us to better connect with VIPs (chronically isolated older people) and volunteers without using traditional face to face methods due to COVID-19 restrictions and their long term impact. This is in response to the significant increase in demand we have seen both in referrals of isolated vulnerable older people, and in requests to get involved in volunteering remotely, since the start of the lock down. The funding would focus on trailblazing work to: - Collaboratively develop a digital training system and platform for volunteers ? allowing us to recruit and train volunteers remotely whilst maintaining our strong sense of community, peer to peer support and fun that is at the core of our work. - Increase and diversify the way we, and our volunteers, communicate with our VIPs - including online, letter, phone and video based support which we can adapt to their individual needs and interests and help encourage confidence to be built as the lock down starts to lift. - Heighten our safeguarding whilst working remotely and maintaining a sense of true friendships being developed - by creating an innovative database system that both staff and volunteers can feed into securely to report red flags and track VIP progress. - Record a set of learnings to support the sector - from collaborating on, testing and implementing of these systems that would benefit the sector as a whole and help other organisations maintain their core values whilst adapting to more remote working. - Employ a much needed temporary member of the team to encourage collaboration and make this happen - a new, fantastic ?Connection Champion? - who would work across the next 6 months to ensure everyone involved in Vintage Vibes was able to contribute to the development of the systems, oversee the testing and implementation of these systems, and ensure that high quality connections were at the centre of everything we do. During this six month period our main aim would be to quickly create high quality approaches that embody the core of what Vintage Vibes is all about ? meaningful connections, quirky individuality, innovative ?out of the box? thinking and setting the foundation for a long term impact. With this in mind, we know that this work across the next six months will not only make a huge difference to enabling us to help as many VIPs and volunteers connect during these unusual times, but will also help us help VIPs re-engage with their communities post COVID, and will make a difference long term to the number of harder to reach, highly vulnerable VIPs and volunteers we are able to engage. It?s win, win, win! Note: Vintage Vibes is a charitable partnership between Space (previously known as Broomhouse Centre and Enterprises) and LifeCare Edinburgh. As the name change from Broomhouse Centre and Enterprises to Space has taken place within the last 12 months, some of our documentation will still refer to Broomhouse Centre and Enterprises.

data.title: Trust Specialist Individual & Group Therapy for People affected by Homelessness
data.description: Many people who are homeless have experienced some form of trauma, often during childhood, and this can have a significant effect on their mental and physical health and act as a major barrier to their attempts to break out of homelessness and move forward in their lives. The Marie Trust provide access to long term counselling for people who are homeless or have experience of homelessness to enable them to work through trauma and recognise how it effects their behaviour and choices so they can resolve their past and thrive. The project provides one to one and group therapy in a range of settings and 50% of clients are women.

data.title: Chrysalis Project
data.description: Receiving refugee status can provide security and safety, but the transition from being an asylum seeker to gaining refugee status can bring its own challenges. The initial 28-day period when people have to rapidly move from one system of support to another can be difficult as they may not be familiar with the systems, may not speak good English and will have to quickly obtain housing. Oasis Cardiff has been supporting refugees and asylum seekers to integrate in Cardiff area and with this investment it will employ two case workers to provide one-to-one support to those recently granted refugee status, to help them navigate housing options, benefit entitlements and employment opportunities.

data.title: Social Bite Housing First Programme
data.description: This Housing First Programme is a major new initiative (launched Aug 2018), which will bring 830 people experiencing homelessness with complex needs into mainstream housing with wrap-around support in five cities: Aberdeen, Dundee, Edinburgh, Glasgow and Stirling. The project aims to shift the structural response to homelessness across Scotland. This funding contributes a small proportion to a much larger project comprised of funds from the Scottish government (£6.5m over 3 years) and significant fundraising from Social Bite (£3m over two years).

data.title: Safer Renting
data.description: Operating out of Cambridge House, based in Southwark, the Safer Renting project offers advice and advocacy to tenants at risk of eviction and living in sub-standard rented properties. Staff work in partnership with local authorities in London to intervene in illegal evictions, support people to sustain tenancies and improve the conditions in their home or find more suitable housing, and to claim their legal rights in the face of criminal landlords. As well as preventing homelessness for vulnerable individuals, the project aims to influence policy to improve conditions for renters and offer greater protection from criminal landlords. Comic Relief will contribute to staff costs and overheads.

data.title: Street Advice Cymru
data.description: Street homelessness in Wales is an increasingly visible and pressing issue. Evidence suggests there has been a 44% increase since 2015. In 2018 there were 345 rough sleepers in Wales. Shelter Cymru has an extensive track record of preventing homelessness using a rights-based approach and with this investment it will employ three Street Advisors to take legal advice and advocacy support onto the streets of Cardiff, Swansea and Wrexham, so that rough sleepers can have access to specialist legal advice about their housing rights. As a result, more rough sleepers can get off the streets and into secure housing as well as access other support services to meet their needs.

data.title: Safe Homes for All
data.description: The Booth Centre is a day centre that offers advice, activities and support to homeless people in Manchester. The Comic Relief funded project 'Safe Homes for All' will support service users to find and keep a secure home, with the right support. The investment will part fund a resettlement worker, a project worker and an evaluation officer. It will also contribute towards the organisation's core costs. Peer mentors (who are or have been homeless) will be trained to work with staff; those who are homeless will be moved into supported or permanent accommodation. The centre will produce a toolkit to share best practise and influence local, national and international stakeholders.

data.title: Housing for Hope
data.description: Vineyard Compassion will establish emergency temporary housing for rough sleepers, who are often housed out side of Coleraine and their communities.On top of this they will provide wraparound support and services that ensure progress to independent and healthy living. They also want support to strengthen their case management system, ensuring they have easily accessible and correct information on the people they support and their needs.

data.title: Preventing homelessness and insecure shelter through direct legal support and advocacy
data.description: The Project aims to provide specialist legal support to children and young people facing homelessness and insecure housing. Justice for Kids Law will recruit a lawyer with expertise in housing and community care law and increase the number of Youth Advocates to 11. The legal specialist will train the Youth Advocates and also provide training and share best practice in the wider voluntary sector. As part of this project, JfKL will explore opportunities for doing strategic litigation for wider reform and identify opportunities for engaging young people in advocacy.

data.title: Preventing Homelessness amongst asylum seekers
data.description: ASAP provide vital work assisting asylum seekers in the UK to access free legal representation at their tribunal appeals. Winning appeals for asylum seekers enables them to access safe and secure shelter, start to rebuild their lives and not be left homeless or at risk of deportation. Funding will also contribute to training other organisations in asylum support law as well as long term systemic change in asylum support policies in the UK ensuring asylum seekers are at less risk of homelessness and insecure shelter. Whilst they are based in London, their work benefits asylum seekers and organisations across the UK.

data.title: Positive Action in Housing Core Funding – Preventing Homelessness in Refugee/BAME Communities
data.description: Positive Action on Housing works with vulnerable and or destitute people from minority ethnic, asylum seeking, refugee or newly arrived migrant communities to access the support and services they need to avoid homelessness and poverty and rebuild their lives. This is done through a hosting scheme that provides accommodation in volunteers homes across the UK while legal issues are resolved, direct advice, support and advocacy to access benefits,and overturn wrong decisions, meeting people's basic needs for food, clothes, hygiene and travel expenses through crisis grants and training and support to improve money and life skills and access employment and sustainable and appropriate housing.

data.title: Universal Credit project
data.description: Child poverty is rising, and housing is one of if not the most significant costs for families. The impact of poverty is insecure, overcrowded homes that deprive children and families of the space they need to play, work and live. The introduction of Universal Credit originally designed to make families better off has had a dramatic effect on the numbers of people becoming homeless. Expert welfare rights advice is crucial to resolving these issues and preventing unnecessary evictions and poverty. This project will equip the advice sector and workers with the knowledge and tools needed navigate the complex benefits system and uphold people's rights and entitlements to financial support.

data.title: Whole Housing: Preventing Homelessness for survivors of Domestic Abuse
data.description: Domestic abuse and housing are intersecting issues; domestic abuse brings violence into the home/ causes women to leave their homes, and a high rate of homeless women have experienced domestic abuse (St Mungo's, 2014). Standing Together Against Domestic Violence (STADV) seeks to improve the response of UK Registered Social Landlords to domestic abuse. It will do this by building on the last two-years of running the Domestic Abuse Housing Alliance (DAHA); this is an alliance of STADV and two UK housing associations (Peabody & Gentoo). Through the DAHA accreditation scheme, the project is seeking Social Landlords to take fast and robust action to support tenants experiencing domestic abuse.

data.title: Exeter Homelessness Partnership
data.description: The Exeter Homelessness Partnership, is a grassroots response aimed at ending homelessness in Exeter. The partnership will bring together people with experience of homelessness with statutory, voluntary, business, and community sectors to increase understanding of the issue and co design community led solutions that everyone can play a part in. This will achieve immediate changes in people's lives and the way support is designed and delivered and lead to structural changes in the way homelessness is addressed and understood. Designed and led by the local community the Partnership will create a Homelessness Charter, Action Groups, test alternative ways of giving and mobilising the public.

data.title: Beyond Grants Pilot
data.description: The purpose of Julian House is to empower our service users to regain control over their lives, develop their skills, resilience and independence, and rebuild a future for themselves and their families after homelessness, domestic abuse, prison, addiction, and long-term unemployment. Last year we provided direct support to over 1,000 individuals with a diverse range of needs.

data.title: Ascension Ventures grant funding
data.description: The Fair by Design Fund (FBDF), which is managed by Ascension Ventures, has been set up to support the growth of ventures that aim to tackle the poverty premium. It invests in ventures ranging from start-ups to high-growth organisations using equity and debt investments to support their growth and scaling of activities. The £50k grant that is being provided to Acension Ventures will go towards supporting a roadshow across the UK with the aim of showcasing existing ventures being supported by the fund, source new ones to support and raise awareness of the poverty premium issue in the UK.

data.title: A helping hand for former prisoners: preventing homelessness after imprisonment abroad
data.description: Prisoners Abroad support British ex-prisoners at high risk of homelessness, who are deported or returning to the UK following imprisonment overseas. Often people have not lived in the UK for many years, have no friends, family or support networks and no access to advice, benefits or housing. People come through the prison gates are put on a plane and arrive at a UK airport with the clothes on their back. Prisoners Abroad provide support to people in the period before release, as well as on return to the UK. They help newly returned ex-prisoners to access advice and emergency resources, housing and the welfare system and to start to rebuild their lives.

data.title: Beyond Grants
data.description: Brent Centre are looking to develop a private service in order to diversify their income and allow them to scale the reach of their existing services to neighbouring boroughs.

data.title: Youth Community Support Agency (YCSA) Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 - Purchase of 8 IPads for use in therapeutic arts activities with young people during lockdown and social distancing. Arts materials to create packs for therapeutic activities which can be dropped to families during lockdown and used for social distanced activities when lockdown is eased. PPE items to ensure safety against COVID eg masks, cleansing wipes etc.- Additional phones, tablets and data due to digital exclusion of many BME young people which leads to their becoming further socially isolated and preventing them accessing support services. YCSA has been successful in obtaining some funding towards this but only until end June ? and we anticipate the need lasting longer. - Contribution towards core costs ? as income streams that helped pay this have dried up during, and in lead up to, lockdown, while costs such as rent, equipment maintenance contracts, standing charges for phones and energy, minibus maintenance, etc. remain.

data.title: England Intermediary Funding Programme
data.description: Groundwork has been selected as Comic Relief's Funding partner to deliver grassroots funding opportunities across England. Groundwork shares Comic Relief’s vision of creating a just world free from poverty and has spent the last four decades building an infrastructure capable of addressing a diverse range of needs in the most disadvantaged local communities across the UK. The funding programme will deliver impact across all areas of England and across each of Comic Relief’s social change priorities through a responsive, demand-led system designed around the needs of grassroots groups and in which decisions are made as close to communities as possible. COVID19 Variation: Additional funding for Covid-19 response awarded via grant 360G-CR-4394874b.

data.title: Build Up London (BUL) Extension
data.description: The Build Up Foundation works with 6-23yr olds in London, many of whom feel stigmatised and excluded from their own community spaces. The first year of the current #iwill grant has enabled it to work with 50 young people on youth-led construction projects - building the skills of young people, and evidencing their value to the wider community. This proposal will involve some of these existing participants in recording their testimonies on film and creating an exhibition to showcase their work. Three-hundred new young people will be involved via youth-led focus groups and as exhibition attendees. The grant will also invest in evaluation support around evidencing social impact..

data.title: Refugee Women: Empower and Change
data.description: Refugee and asylum-seeking women are some of the most vulnerable women in the UK. They are often isolated and frequently dispersed into areas where they cannot access appropriate support. The majority will suffer from past trauma from experiencing gender-based violence. They have to go through the asylum process that is seen as hostile and combative, leaving them disempowered and at risk of destitution. With this investment, Women for Refugee Women and Refugee Women Connect will support women to build their confidence and skills to share their experience, advocate for their rights and to speak out for the need for a fairer asylum process in the UK.

data.title: ‘Could Do Better’: Pushing for a “whole school approach” to girls’ safety and equality
data.description: This request is to to build on and continue the End Violence Against Women coalition's (EVAW) strategic work on tackling violence against girls and young women in schools. The 'Whole School Approach' uses a number of approaches including targeted policy change at government level, and enabling better support for grassroots involvement at a local level. EVAW have begun to do some of the top-level work already, and this funding will contribute mainly to extending the frontline involvement with local women's organisations, teachers, affected girls and their families.

data.title: Building the Women’s Centre Movement
data.description: WIP wants to harness the power of the lived experience of women caught in the criminal justice system to shift the harmful social narratives & structural inequalities that disproportionately disadvantage them.WIP proposes to support women to develop skills & confidence to take up space in spheres of social and political influence, to engage those who hold power over the resources channelled towards meeting their needs (media, commissioners and government ministers), to bring adequate and sustainable funding to realise the Female Offender Strategy.

data.title: Women's Lives Leeds (WLL) VOICES
data.description: The aim of Women’s Lives Leeds VOICES is for Leeds to become the UK’s first Women Friendly City. The aim would be to create changes to how women and girls see and experience Leeds as a place to live, across many aspects of their lives. That Leeds will be a place where women are at the heart of decision making and are influencing the design, commissioning and planning of services, and where services and activities promote gender equality. The work will be led and galvanised through two ‘hubs’ which will engage women and girls and ensure their voices are heard. A Campaign Manager will help to take forward activities and build wider support.

data.title: Equal Power
data.description: The Fawcett Society will run the 'Equal Power' Project helping more women to stand for local and national elected office with a goal of having more women in positions of political power to break the current gender disparity in politics (only 30% MP's and 33% local councillors are women). The aim is to increase formal power for women in the UK. Including their #Askhertostand campaign, the Equal Power project will work with 5 other organisations in partnership to provide training, preparation and support to women to ensure they are equipped with the skills, confidence, experience and networks to succeed in running and hopefully winning local and national elections.

data.title: A National Movement of Equality for Young Women and Work
data.description: The Young Women's Trust across three years will form a national (UK) movement of young women (18-30 years old) who will tackle the barriers facing young women in accessing, sustaining and progressing in employment. This will be largely led by their youth advisory board of 30 young women driving the approach to change. This grant is towards both project and core costs, and activities will be centred around supporting young women to take collaborative and individual actions towards greater gender equality in the workplace. This is through both interaction with decision makers and media, but also through equipping them with transferable skills in leadership, teamwork & communication at work.

data.title: Rose Vouchers for Fruit & Veg Project (RVP)
data.description: Rose Vouchers for Fruit and Veg Programme (RVP) supports families on low incomes to avoid food poverty & access a healthy diet by providing vouchers for fresh fruit & veg redeemable only at local markets & community food projects. Since their first Tech for Good grant to fund the 'Rosie' trader reimbursement app, they've embarked on an exciting digital transformation journey with partners Neontribe, continually engaging users/beneficiaries to build & refine tech that responds to their needs. RVP is a proven intervention currently supporting 1000+ families through a network of 26 children’s centres in 6 local authority areas.

data.title: Breathing Space
data.description: Survivors of domestic and sexual abuse can struggle to meet their mental health support needs when faced with services that are not trauma-informed; many services have long waiting lists and cannot provide support 24/7. AVA and its digital tech partner Infact will design and build an app to meet these womens' needs; the digital product will give users immediate relief through functions that could include trauma-informed-meditation, and tips around coping strategies. The project will test assumptions about what survivors want/ need through the use of a Steering Group of 'experts by experience'. This user-group will be involved for the duration of the project from scoping through to launch.

data.title: Virtually Minded
data.description: The extension to the Virtually Minded project will develop the delivery method to better engage and support 10-12 year olds from the Falcon Lodge estate, Sutton Coldfield and Conker Island estate, Kingstanding. A mobile youth bus will visit the estates and weekly sessions will encourage small groups of young men to participate in range of activities. The young men will be supported to better understand mental health, and encouraged to develop their own social media and Comic-Con campaign helping them to develop a range of practical and social skills. A grant will support the costs of youth workers, consultation and delivery, plus a contribution to management and organisational overheads.

recipientOrganization.name: Sutton Coldfield Young Mens Christian Association

data.title: WAVES (Wellbeing Awarness and Voice for East Surrey) Meet and Eat project
data.description: Younger children are increasingly experiencing mental health problems such as social anxiety, low self-esteem and depression. They often find it difficult to talk to parents/caregivers about their mental health, and parents often feel unequipped to deal with and support children at home. YMCA East Surrey has been working with older youth to help them manage their own mental health and become mental health champions, raising awareness of mental health in their communities. Those mental health champions have proposed this 'meet and eat' project to work with younger children age 9-11 and parents. As a result, children and parents will both be better equipped to deal with issues as they arise.

data.title: Citz Young Storytellers
data.description: Cardboard Citizens support young people from London who have been affected by or are at risk of homelessness. Citz Young Storytellers is a young people-led, arts-based approach, to ensure disengaged and disadvantaged young people’s stories are heard and valued. Through workshops and performance they will develop creative, soft and transferable skills and make their voice heard on the issues that effect them. This grant will mainly pay for staff to support and engage the young people, including employing young people with lived experience of homelessness to support others. The project will support young people’s long-term independence, confidence & progression as social activists.

data.title: Fundamentals Expansion
data.description: Small Green Shoots will develop the FundaMentals projects to initially support an additional 140 young people in London who are from deprived communities, and mostly not in education, employment and training. Through arts-based projects the young people will explore mental health, developing their understanding and a range of skills whilst being supported by a freelance artist. Through this development the delivery model will also be piloted in 2 sites outside of London, supporting 60 young people, and an online toolkit will be developed and marketed by the young people, which can then be used freely by other youth-led organisations. Funding will support staffing and delivery costs.

data.title: Holistic Needs Assessment (HNA) Portal
data.description: Muscular Dystrophy UK are the leading organisation supporting at least 70,000 people living with a range of muscle wasting conditions in the UK. The project is looking to work in partnership with Sitekit to develop an online Holistic Needs Assessment portal (HNA), where people living with these conditions can conduct their own wellbeing assessments, which will make it easier for NCAs (Neuromuscular Care Advisors) to manage their care plans, reduce the risk of side-lining issues such as mental health, and enable them to be signposted more quickly to tailored services. There are only 60 NCAs, each managing the care plans of about 500 patients.

data.title: Intelligent chat bot - 24 hour support for young people seeking mental health support
data.description: The Mix are looking to develop chatbot technology that allows them to create a bespoke experience for individuals that hit their channels. This is in order to ensure that they are able to serve a higher percentage of youth that reach them, that users find what they are looking for and that there is better signposting to other services/offerings, and to digitize their outreach and engagement to youth on channels that they use most frequently.

data.title: a smart phone app to help young people manage symptoms of depression
data.description: Stem4 provides education in secondary schools in four areas of mental health. These include anxiety & depression, self-harm, eating disorders and addiction. Building on the success of their NHS-accredited ‘Calm Harm’ app (helping teenagers manage the urge to self-harm), as well as the previously Tech for Good-funded ‘Clear Fear’ app (helping teenagers manage anxiety), STEM4 will develop a third app which will use a third model of Behavioural Activation therapy to help teenagers manage symptoms of depression. The target groups of the app are those with a diagnosis, those waiting for treatment, and those turned away from services.

data.title: Experts by Experience
data.description: The project will work in North Tyneside with young adult carers, male young carers and bereaved young carers to identify how improvements can be made in services for these groups. A Research Facilitator will recruit young carers, who will act as Experts by Experience. They will be supported to identify and communicate what improvements they want to see. The project will also engage internal and external decision makers to act on young people’s ideas. Young carers will gain confidence, skills and experience but the project also aims to make lasting change in the way these young people are engaged and supported locally. The grant will pay for staffing, activities and project overheads.

data.title: Bipolar Chatbot
data.description: According to research conducted by Bipolar UK (the only charity specifically focused on bipolar) there are 1.3 million people living with bipolar in the UK. They propose a chatbot that helps users self manage but also provides critical advice. The chatbot combines machine learning with the informed research from Bipolar UK, by giving answers, prompts and signposting users to information. This funding will scale up the chatbot by installing it on the website, integrating it with services, so people can book a call with a volunteer or attend a group, and ensure staff with lived experience can keep it up dated.

data.title: Sitting & Befriending website
data.description: Ruils will transform its highly successful Sitting & Befriending service, which matches trained befrienders to disabled children in South-West London. It is currently admin heavy and based in office hours, limiting the number of children they can support and creating difficulties in engaging time-poor parents of disabled children. The grant will develop a new website which will empower parents, carers and children to engage directly with the service. This will remove a huge amount of admin, enabling Ruils staff to significantly expand the service, meaning more befrienders can help disabled children to enjoy activities, gain some independence & practice social skills.

data.title: Lived Experience to Leading Change
data.description: Care-experienced young people can feel that 'corporate parents' - the term for agencies designed to support their care - fail to appreciate the challenges they face. While the first #iwill grant was about the broad recruitment of members for Voices From Care, this grant will build on the organisation's work to influence policy/ practice. The project will enable care experienced young people to come together in small groups (based on location or issue) to work on social action campaigns that will help to influence corporate parents. For example, a group of care experienced young people in North Wales may create a pod-cast aimed at changing a referral practice within a housing team.

data.title: DeafKidz Defenders
data.description: DeafKidz International (DKI) is a young organisation working to address the safeguarding and protection needs of Deaf, hard of D/deaf CYP, and are emerging as leaders in this space. They are proposing to develop DeafKidz Defender, an interactive digital game concept that will empower Deaf children aged 7-11 to reduce their risk and vulnerability to abuse and exploitation. There is currently no dedicated digital safeguarding and protection provision specifically aimed at Deaf children of this age in the UK or worldwide.

data.title: Weall
data.description: Weall is a creative project led by young people that will use a variety of creative genres to educate, raise awareness and reduce stigma around mental health issues. The project works in St Ann’s, one of Nottingham’s most deprived inner city communities and will work over 8 months with young people to research, design and develop a combination of various creative pieces which will use hip-hop, rap, grime, spoken word, dance, film photography, poetry and podcasts. The project will develop the young participants’ skills and confidence, whilst raising mental health awareness in the wider community.

data.title: Team Up
data.description: This project will target young people in Coventry who are newly arrived, in care, or have faced gender violence - the common thread is that these young people often find it hard to feel part of a community. This grant will fill a gap within Positive Youth Foundation for a move-on stage (from the first #iwill grant) for graduates from these target groups. Graduates will be able to apply to undertake a Youth Achievement Bronze Award. Participants will then utilise this training by working in groups as 'Youth Consultants' for local youth providers; they will do this by undertaking social research and action planning with their young service users to help improve youth services.

data.title: Reaching Further Into Communities: Supporting BAME/PoC LGBT Young People to Engage in Social Action
data.description: Across the UK, LGBT young people face discrimination, bullying and violence throughout their life: in school, their workplace, home and community. These threats can be particularly pronounced for young people who identify as Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic and/or People of Colour (BAME/PoC) and those within faith groups. This project will support LGBT BAME/PoC young people in the Midlands and North of England to engage in social action within their communities. Supported by Stonewall, participants will work to design and deliver campaigns to challenge discrimination and build support for LGBT rights within their local area, bringing change in their lives and the lives of others.

data.title: Investment proposal for Social and Sustainable Housing LP Housing Fund
data.description: The SASC Housing Fund will look to invest into properties that will then be leased to a range of charities and social enterprises that are in need of homes to deliver their services. The aim of the fund is to provide a solution to these organisations when it comes to buying property, support them in building their financial capacity by enabling them to acquire assets and grow their impact by enabling them to work with vulnerable people.· Meet the needs of investors who are looking to do good, manage risk and achieve an appropriate level of return.

data.title: Portrait of Britain
data.description: Joseph Roundtree Foundation (JRF) are working with an award-winning photographer and the writer to gather stories of poverty which challenge the stereotype, not through righteousness outrage, which can alienate people across the ideological divide, but by portraying poverty as everyone’s business, asking ‘what could you not live without’. The work is still ongoing, but the collection of stories so far gathered range from the extraordinary to the ordinary, highlighting the commonality between all of us as human beings. JRF would like to turn the stories into a touring exhibition to be launched in London and then travelling to key regions throughout the

data.title: Sharing Space Increasing Power
data.description: This grant will enable the development of the Women’s March London to unite, empower and mobilise the next generation of intersectional feminists in the UK. We will work with members, partners and supporters to create a visionary democratic structure that represents and supports women from the grassroots to challenge power, create change and heal.

data.title: Luminary Bakery Ltd
data.description: Luminary Bakery is looking to expand its successful bakery service which works with vulnerable women and provides them with employment and support. They have identified a new site in London to expand into and have raised 75% of the funding required for the move (the investment will go towards refurbishing the site, hiring staff, getting equipment and providing funds for the launch). The new bakery will enable Luminary to further grow its income and to work with more vulnerable women by offering them employment.

data.title: RainbowSports@Mind
data.description: Rainbow Sports@Mind will gather London’s diverse LGBTQ+ community within a safe supportive mental health focused environment. The service will run twice weekly with user selected activities including dance, yoga, walking, boxing and football, offering users a chance to get together and collectively work towards goals of improved mental health. Following sessions, users will be signposted to other Mind services, and will also have the opportunity to be trained as volunteers, so they can facilitate the sessions beyond the programme.

data.title: Young Peace Leaders
data.description: This project will train young adults in Newham, London as Peace Leaders, using the power of football to bring disparate communities together and offer targeted integration activities for children and young adults in the Borough. Using a peer mentor approach, the programme will help youth in Newham come together and aims to help overcome challenges such as rising crime, drug use, racial division and religious extremism. Peace Leaders are identified by peers, schools and community structures and are provided with an assessed 12 week training course before being supported to design and run social football tournaments with children and young adults in their communities.

data.title: Sport for Change: supporting asylum seekers and refugees at the heart of our community
data.description: Refugees and asylum seekers are often cut-off from the community because of barriers including: language, destitution, and a lack of networks. Islington Centre for Refugees and Migrants helps to integrate this vulnerable group into community life. It has already trialled the use of sport; now - in partnership with Mary's Community Centre (MCC) - this project will run weekly sports sessions including boxing and yoga. Sport will be a pathway to help this isolated group to access MCC's 'community hub'; building connections with local residents and linking them with MCC's Community Development Worker. Sport will also be a vehicle for 'community language learning' to build English skills.

recipientOrganization.name: Islington Centre for Refugees and Migrants

data.title: Core Sport and Core Arts: using activity and creativity to support social integration
data.description: People with mental health problems often experience social isolation. The Core Sports programme provides access to a wide range of sport and physical activity sessions, social events and art activities/qualifications to adults with mild to severe mental health needs. The programme will build social networks, and clients will see an improvement in their mental and physical health. Over 2 years the programme will work with 500+ adults from across London from their creative education centre in Hackney.

data.title: Sporting Memories London Together
data.description: Sporting Memories will increase the mental & physical wellbeing of 250 people over the age of 50, using the power of sport as a focus to engage those who are living with dementia, depression or are socially isolated in sports reminiscence & physical exercise in 6 weekly clubs across London. The six clubs will focus on engaging members of the Irish, Jewish and BAME communities. In addition to weekly sessions, young people from across schools and colleges will support the delivery of the reminiscence sessions and carry out interviews, which will be used to create artwork to be displayed in the schools and clubs. Young and older people will come together for the 'London Together Games'.

data.title: Get Onside
data.description: Young Offenders have often lived complicated & chaotic lives. They represent some of the most socially excluded, vulnerable & disadvantaged young people in England. The Get Onside project provides sport, education and life skills within Feltham Young Offenders Institute, with the aim of reducing reoffending and creating positive members of local communities. This investment will part fund the Get Onside project to work with 80 young offenders over two years.

data.title: Stepping Out
data.description: Stepping out will provide structured sporting activities (football and walking) for migrants, refugees and asylum seekers. These activities will integrate ESOL (English for Speakers of Other Languages) and sport, in an engaging way, with participants learning the key words related to the activity. Participants can attend the weekly walk and talk club at Walthamstow Wetlands, or football at Tottenham FC, with the activity followed by a debrief at Consonant HQ. This project targets communities who are increasingly isolated, due to the hostile society, barriers to work and limited English, the intervention will allow them to integrate in a more natural environment, whilst improving English.

data.title: All Together - Deaf Londoners Activation Programme
data.description: Deaf people often face barriers in accessing services and support. This includes sport and physical activity, with only 10% of the deaf and hard of hearing population physically active. UK Deaf Sport (UKDS) will recruit and train deaf activator champions to support deaf people to access sporting and non sporting activities in their community, increasing access opportunities and reducing isolation.

data.title: Team Up Take Part
data.description: In Rotherhithe, South London, there has been a rapid influx of new residents who have little knowledge of the local community or connection to it. There is a presumption that this group is self-sufficient and independent, but they can lack friendships and long term connections regardless of their achievements in their professional lives. There is also an ongoing problem around isolated vulnerable/older people. Team Up Take Part will bring people together from all backgrounds through a sport-based befriending programme that will encourage socially isolated people to build connections with their local community and make use out of local green/open spaces and other community assets.

data.title: Thriving after Economic Abuse
data.description: SEA/MAP have identified the problem that people don't know what economic abuse is, or that help is available. There is a lack of knowledge and support and some of the generic advice available does not take safety into account. SEA have already created a screening tool to identify economic abuse. They want to transform this into a digital tool that will analyse responses and direct people to the resources they need and which are tailored to their situation. This will provide safe and up to date information to survivors of economic abuse as well as to professionals supporting them. It will also be found easily, even when the person does not know what they are experiencing is economic abuse.

data.title: Helping Hand- children and young people over coming domestic abuse
data.description: Research has highlighted concerns over the emotional wellbeing of children who have experienced abuse with many young people believing the abuse was their fault. There is limited support for young people and particularly a lack of age appropriate and trauma-informed support.AVA will co-produce a digital product with young people who have experienced abuse. The product will be available to young people throughout the country to support them to recover from their experiences, help them rebuild their lives and address mental health issues. The grant will pay for staff to work with the young people on co-production and technical support to develop the product.

data.title: MySayMyWay
data.description: The idea is to create a women's portal, enabling women to access their own user area, managing and increasing their control over their journey when they are accessing The Haven's services. This will give them greater control on both the type of support they access, and how and when they access it. The focus will be on women staying safe, accessing the right advice and information whenever they need it. At the core of this grant is a user-centered design approach.

data.title: Accessible information & earlier intervention: using digital to better support survivors
data.description: The information available on domestic abuse is fragmented and hard to find. Women who do not recognise they are in an abusive relationship do not search for information in a way that leads them to the right information. WAFE's survivors handbook is online but it is not found by those who need it and, when found, the format and language do not resonate with women who have a preference for video, audio and bitesize information that they can access on their phone. This grant will support WAFE to develop a prototype of a new resource which is interactive, accessible and optimised for digital use, in order to reach more women, more effectively at an earlier stage.

data.title: Resilience - So That We Are Stronger
