data.title: Basketball Health Corps: Improving Mental Health Through Sport
data.description: Shooting Touch, in collaboration with community-based partners, will use the power of sport (basketball) to improve Rwandan individuals? knowledge and management of mental health. Shooting Touch will also strive to reduce the existing stigmas, on an individual, family, and community level, around the understanding and treatment of people with poor mental health.

grantProgramme.title: Ahead of the Game: Sport and Mental Health

data.title: Sporting Memories Network CIC Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -We would like funding to support our core costs and costs we are incurring outside of project funds we have received. This will allow us to continue to reach out to older people through a range of activities linked to sports reminiscence and physical activity to help reduce isolation, improve mental well-being and physical health. Activities created to date are stated within 2.3.
 
 We would spend the additional funding from Comic Relief on:
 
 Communications - to reach out to isolated individuals who cannot attend clubs, as well as their families. We would also reach out to new potential beneficiaries and future attendees of Sporting Memories Clubs that are face to face, when we can safely reopen.
 
 Data collection ? gathering data for contact to individuals and building a CRM system as well as data for evidence of the impact we are having for older people during this pandemic. 
 
 Physical products/resources to send to individuals without technology therefore, who cannot download digital resources. This may be a weekly printed Sporting Pink or small physical equipment for low level exercises. 
 
 Continuing of producing and developing the National Sporting Pink - which will support opening out to a wider public.
 
 Marketing support to reach new partners ? For example working with Housing Associations, other charities with direct older people contact to share resources and signpost to activities.

data.title: Restoring Children and Young People's Lost Aspiration, Integrity and Mental Well-being (ReCLAIM)
data.description: It is estimated that around 20% of the population of Zambia experience mental disorders and 3% of will experience severe disorder. There is stigma associated with having a mental illness and children and young people experiencing problems are often feared, marginalised and labelled. Provision of mental health support is patchy and there are barriers in seeking help. SOS Children’s Villages Zambia, in partnership with REPSSI, will deliver psychosocial training programmes in schools and communities so that they have the skills and confidence to identify and intervene early so children and young people who are experiencing or at risk of developing mental health problems can access support.

grantProgramme.title: Bridging the Gaps: Strengthening Mental Health Support for Children and Young People

data.title: Community-Based Mental Health Services for Children and Young People in Marginalised Communities.
data.description: The project will be focusing on the provision of Mental Health (MH) support to children, adolescents and youth (5-30 yr olds) in under-served, remote and disaster-prone communities. A quality and inclusive community-based MH support system will be developed to strengthen MH health knowledge and skills of families, DPOs, local government representatives, health providers and teachers. This training will be rooted in stigma reduction with different stakeholders; strengthening community networks to support individuals with MH, signposting them to quality support and advocating for adequate resources to support implementation of the MH Act 2018 (0.5%< of the health budget is allocated for MH).

grantProgramme.title: Bridging the Gaps: Strengthening Mental Health Support for Children and Young People

data.title: BALANCED: Improving the wellbeing of key populations in Kigali City through sport
data.description: The project in Kigali will establish a yoga and mental health programme for youth at risk/experiencing mental distress. Target groups include young people living with HIV, sex workers, and LGBTQ young people. The programme will also improve livelihoods and reduce social stigma. Partnerships with Amahoro Respect and United Purpose will expand the project’s reach, impact and learning in the wider sector.

grantProgramme.title: Ahead of the Game: Sport and Mental Health

data.title: Strong Bodies, Strong Minds: Matupi Amphamvu, Maganizo Amphamvu
data.description: Young people living with HIV represent an underserved population that face complex health challenges, barriers to services as well as stigma and social exclusion, all of which has an impact on their mental health. Grassroot Soccer Zambia, in partnership with Strong Minds, will pilot an integrated, youth friendly programme of support to young people living with HIV. The model will train young coaches and community based young adult mentors who are openly living with HIV and well-versed in using sport-based programmes, to begin to use mental health psychosocial support using Interpersonal Group Therapy (IPT-G).

grantProgramme.title: Bridging the Gaps: Strengthening Mental Health Support for Children and Young People

data.title: Engaging and Enabling Youth to Address Suicide Prevention in India
data.description:
In 2016, India accounted for 36.6% in women and 24.4% in men of world suicides (Dandona, 2018). This proposal is a partnership between a mental health organisation, a law college and a tech company to deliver a three pronged rights based approach to fill the gaps in mental health awareness and services: 
  - Youth engagement campaign to raise awareness.
  - Peer counselling service through a digitally assisted programme.
  - Young People advocating for mental health policy change
  The project will address mental health stigma, encourage help-seeking behaviour, provide much needed support to those experiencing distress and campaign for better service provisions from the state.

grantProgramme.title: Bridging the Gaps: Strengthening Mental Health Support for Children and Young People

data.title: Freeing African communities from the deadly threat of malaria in Uganda and Kenya and addressing the vulnerabilities of Adolescent Girls and Young Women (AGYW) in Malawi.
data.description: This proposal forms part of Comic Relief's funding agreement with the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. BMGF's $10m grant to Comic Relief as part of RND19 campaign is being matched by Comic Relief 1:1 and split 50/50 between The Global Fund and The Challenge Initiative.We have previously funded The Global Fund to deliver work focused on malaria within the ECD age range. This year we are introducing another element, focusing on reducing HIV transmission among adolescent women and young girls.

recipientOrganization.name: The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria

data.title: Bridging the Gaps: Mental Health Support for Out of School Adolescents in Urban Slums in Kenya
data.description: The project will pilot and evaluate mental health training into an evidence-based social, health and economic asset building program (safe spaces) and work with out-of-school girls and boys aged 15-18 living in informal settlements and are living in extreme poverty, have limited access to services and increased risk of violence. The project will work in Rhonda in Nakru and Kariobangi to address stigmatisation of mental health in adolescents, increase awareness on warning signs of mental illness and provide basic counselling.

grantProgramme.title: Bridging the Gaps: Strengthening Mental Health Support for Children and Young People

data.title: Open Minds: children & young people overcoming mental health problems caused by skin NTDs in Nigeria
data.description: This proposal is a partnership between The Leprosy Mission England, The Leprosy Mission Nigeria and Gede Foundation. Working together, they aim to support children and young people(CYP) living with leprosy and neglected tropical diseases (NTD) with their mental health problems. Depression is reported in up to 50% of leprosy patients (Mangeard-Lourme J, 2018) and 20% of lymphatic filariasis patients in Nigeria (Obindo et al., 2017). The project will work with controlled peer support groups, where CYP can discuss their mental health and NTDs, and access professional mental health support with Gede Foundation referring on those that need specialist support.

grantProgramme.title: Bridging the Gaps: Strengthening Mental Health Support for Children and Young People

data.title: Initiative for Mental Health Care and Support to the children of most excluded communities
data.description: Children survivors of sexual abuse and those from marginalised castes and communities will experience mental health problems as a result of the hardship, trauma and prejudices they face. In some communities children may be ostracised or blamed if they speak up about the sexual abuse they have experienced. Jan Sahas are training up 'barefoot counsellors' (non professionals given training) to provide mental health support in these marginalised communities. They will create counselling hubs led by psychologists to provide professional support, raise awareness within the communities, and train staff working in this space to provide a more trauma informed approach to these groups

grantProgramme.title: Bridging the Gaps: Strengthening Mental Health Support for Children and Young People

data.title: From the Ground Up: Tackling Stigma and Providing Essential Mental Health Services for the Rohingya
data.description: This project aims to build the individual and collective resilience of 1470 Rohingya children (6-12) and 1470 adolescent refugees (13-24) in refugee camps through addressing the stigma surrounding Mental Health (MH) amongst young people and their communities through the provision of safe spaces, and community education. MH services will be integrated in the approach to respond to their urgent psychosocial needs. The proposal aims to target 735 Rohingya adolescent girls, recognising social norms often leads to their reduced mobility and thus, being excluded from interventions and 735 boys who often use negative coping mechanisms such as drug taking in lieu of access to quality MH provision.

grantProgramme.title: Bridging the Gaps: Strengthening Mental Health Support for Children and Young People

data.title: Community Foundation Ireland - Intermediary Fund
data.description: Community Foundation Ireland act as an Intermediary Funder for Comic Relief. CFI distribute funds raised in Ireland through an annual St Patrick's Day comedy gig to charities working with young homeless people and young refugees and asylum seekers in Ireland and internationally.

data.title: Safeguarding hope: mental health and psychosocial support for refugee families and frontline workers
data.description: Refugee Trauma Initiative will run their two main programmes for young people and children (with their parents) of refugee and asylum seeker status. Funding will cover 3 years of a proportion of their core costs in Greece, where they operate in 6 regions. RTI works with refugees and asylum seekers, as well as young people from the local communities to provide psycho-social care through its community based approach in it's Baytna early childhood development model. RTI also runs skills training through the use of media and arts for young people between 15-24 (Dinami), to help them build a community network and support them as they transition to adulthood, through a trauma informed approach.

grantProgramme.title: ACROSS BORDERS: Routes to safety for refugees

data.title: Uprooted and Unprotected: Supporting Young People in their Search for Safety
data.description: RYS is applying for core funds to further its rights-based work improving the safety and wellbeing of unaccompanied minors and youth on the move. In Northern France (Calais and Dunkirk), they will empower locally registered organisations to carry the current work forward, and strengthen the coordination between key child protection actors to uphold childrens' rights. RYS is expanding and diversifying its governance structure to better guide and support current and future operations. In Athens, they will continue through their partner Velos Youth to run a youth centre focused on supporting young people's long term holistic needs, including finding long term accommodation.

grantProgramme.title: ACROSS BORDERS: Routes to safety for refugees

data.title: AMAN أمان – SAFETY Human Trafficking Prevention Partnership Across Borders
data.description: Syrian refugees and asylum seekers are at high risk of human trafficking in areas of Greece and Turkey. Stop the Traffik will use their tested methodology to influence a change in awareness, knowledge and behaviours to reduce trafficking. Social media initiatives are collaboratively created and locally-led, engaging international stakeholders to raise awareness of specific types of exploitation of Syrian refugees & asylum seekers, keeping them safe of human trafficking while making the environment high risk & low profit for traffickers. Local community partners will be identified, worked with, and also trained to recognise potential trafficking situations and how to prevent them.

grantProgramme.title: ACROSS BORDERS: Routes to safety for refugees

data.title: Education Plus: Meaningful education for refugee youth in Egypt
data.description: This project will provide education services to refugee children and youth in Cairo in Egypt while providing other essential support that contributes to a meaningful learning environment in an unstable context. StARS will integrate five types of support to education, namely financial, legal, psychosocial, medical, and mental health support. They provide technical expertise, training and financial support to community schools and hubs set up and run by refugees in communities throughout the city, developing an essential infrastructure of support. Finally they work in partnership with the refugee communities and key partner organisations to advocate for change and improved service provision

grantProgramme.title: ACROSS BORDERS: Routes to safety for refugees

data.title: Routes to safety for stateless refugees
data.description: To be stateless is not to be recognised as a national by any country in the world. Caused by state succession, gaps in nationality laws, discrimination, displacement, and nationality stripping, statelessness is a legal anomaly with devastating impact on access to rights, safety and belonging. With this investment, European Network on Stateless will work to protect the rights of stateless refugees and prevent children being born stateless in Europe. It will gather evidence of the impact of statelessness, build the capacity of civil society and relevant authorities and run a campaign to mobilise and inspire action.

grantProgramme.title: ACROSS BORDERS: Routes to safety for refugees

data.title: Developing (Re)Integration Tools for Children on the Move
data.description: Children on the move in Northern Europe, Turkey, Greece and Lebanon are at increased risk of family separation as they make the often-perilous journey from their home country to countries where they can be safe. It leaves them at risk of exploitation, abuse, violence, trafficking and death. Family for Every Child supports children to grow up in safe and caring families or appropriate alternative care where this is not possible. With this investment, it will carry out research, generate learning and develop tools so that agencies can help children reintegrate with their families in a safe way. The tools will also provide guidance to help children integrate into their host communities.

grantProgramme.title: ACROSS BORDERS: Routes to safety for refugees

data.title: Speak Your Mind – South Africa Campaign
data.description: The South African Speak Your Mind (SYM) Campaign targets the general public, government and key role players as well as communities at grassroots level to ensure the most comprehensive impact possible. This proposal is aimed at (a) producing SYM information and (b) promotional materials, to be utilised and disseminated during (c) provincial community engagement events. We would also like to (d) document the ‘evolution’ of the campaign through short but informative, professionally produced videos.

recipientOrganization.name: South African Federation for Mental Health

data.title: Save Life: Speak up for Suicide Prevention
data.description: The project is designed to influence policy level intervention for suicide prevention in Nepal and contribute to the development of National Strategy on Suicide Prevention appropriate for the current context. The project will be implemented form October 2019 to September 2020. The project will be jointly implemented by KOSHISH and TPO Nepal, complementing each other to achieve the results set forward by the project. The project will prioritize the multisectoral involvement in suicide prevention through involvement of various social organizations and governments for the cause.

data.title: “‘Ghana Speak Your Mind for Mental Health Reform’ campaign”
data.description: The “‘Speak Your Mind!’ for Mental Health in Ghana” is a national campaign to increase the prioritisation of mental health in Ghana. The project combines mass mobilisation with targeted engagements to build an advocacy platform that will (1) enhance public knowledge and awareness on mental health and amplify the voice of mental health service users and carers advocating for their needs and rights; (2) To ensure decision-makers in Ghana increase funding for mental health; and (3) have the Legislative Instrument of the Mental Health Law (Act 846, 2012) approved and implemented in the country.

data.title: Open the space and start the discussion on Mental Health
data.description: Funding will support the Mental Health Coalition Sierra Leone to influence the Government’s commitment and political will for the prioritization of Mental Health financing and implementing workable Mental Health policy. The MHC will advocate for the review of existing outdated legislation and will provide capacity building and awareness raising to challenge stigma and discrimination via its network of people with lived experience who will work with family members, service providers and other stake holders including faith based groups and traditional leaders that will uphold people’s rights and promote inclusion, equal and non - discriminatory participation for people.

data.title: Strengthening the Refugee & Migrants' Rights Movement in the Euro Mediterranean
data.description: Refugee and migrants ‘rights groups working at grassroots level are usually under-resourced and isolated from each other. Funding tends to focus largely on humanitarian aid or integration projects in Europe with little or no funding to reach vulnerable people during their migration journey, particularly with a human rights lens. With this investment, The Fund for Global Human Rights will make grants to 8-10 small groups in the Euro Mediterranean region, mainly Morocco and the Spanish enclave of Melilla, who are working to promote and protect refugee and migrants’ rights. It will also help the groups to build their capacity, work collaboratively and share learning with each other.

grantProgramme.title: ACROSS BORDERS: Routes to safety for refugees

recipientOrganization.name: Fund for Global Human Rights UK

data.title: A Safe Journey Home – reuniting refugee children with their families
data.description: Thousands of refugee children and families continue to take desperate journeys to Europe. Many unaccompanied and separated children who have escaped persecution and conflict in countries such as Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan now find themselves in cities and detention centres in transit countries such as Egypt, Libya, Ethiopia and Sudan. With this investment UNHCR, with its partners International Refugee Assistance Project (IRAP) and RefugePoint, will deliver ‘A Safe Journey Home’ project to provide legal pathways for child and youth in Egypt, Libya, Ethiopia and Sudan so that they can be safely reunited with their families and to reduce the need for them to take dangerous routes to Europe.

grantProgramme.title: ACROSS BORDERS: Routes to safety for refugees

data.title: Increased access to legal assistance for asylum seekers on Samos (Greece)
data.description: European Lawyers in Lesvos wish to replicate their model of access to free legal assistance for asylum seekers and refugees on the Greek Island of Samos. Support will operate close to the refugee camp the team is made up of full time staff and volunteers, who are specilaist lawyers and interpreters able to deliver this service to those needing assistance for their asylum and refugee claims. \r European Lawyers will also work in partnership with KIND (kids in need of defence) to advocate for legal and policy reform at the EU level, as well as use bespoke technology implemented by KIND to facilitate remote access to legal assistance for refugees and asylum seekers who are on the move.

grantProgramme.title: ACROSS BORDERS: Routes to safety for refugees

data.title: IMARISHA MENTAL HEALTH INTEGRATED INITIATIVE
data.description: A third of Kenyans under the age of 30 experience mental health problems and most mental illnesses start before the age of 18. There are few services for people with mental health problems, and high levels of stigma. This project will promote mental health and wellbeing in schools and communities, train health workers on quality care for and rights of people with mental health problems, and train and support mental health champions to identify people with mental health problems and refer them to care. The project will press for greater levels of funding for mental health services. The project will take place in Kisumu and Vihiga counties.

grantProgramme.title: Improving Mental Health and Wellbeing in Kenya

data.title: Arts, Pop Culture & Social Change
data.description: Based on the highly successful Refugee Week model, Counterpoints Arts will commission artists from refugee communities in UK, Greece and Germany to produce public works of art that spark interest, discussion and engagement by the public about perceptions and realities of being a refugee in 2020 Europe. The project will support individuals from refugee backgrounds though a leadership programme, develop a network of arts based organisations across Europe to increase representation and inclusion of refugee artists and shift public opinion, understanding and attitudes though engagement with a range of different art works and storytelling.

grantProgramme.title: ACROSS BORDERS: Routes to safety for refugees

data.title: Bridging the Gaps: Strengthening Mental Health Support for Children and Young People
data.description: IsraAID are proposing to set up mobile child friendly spaces (CFS) so they can deliver health and wellbeing activities to underserved children in refugee camp and settlement areas; strengthen the capacity of children as agents of their own protection by mentoring and building the capacity of child champions focused on public speaking, child rights and mental health; strengthen the capacity of parents, caregivers and community members to respond to child protection issues; raise awareness of the availability of mental health services; and refer patients experiencing mental health issues to services which can help, in Turkana county.

grantProgramme.title: Improving Mental Health and Wellbeing in Kenya

data.title: Moving the Story On - Changing public attitudes to people on the move through participatory arts
data.description: Good Chance Theatre uses arts as a means of welcome and integration, empower refugee artists, strengthen communities and tell the human stories behind global migration. With this investment, it will develop a new production, The Walk, which involves a 12-foot-high puppet representing a refugee child, Little Amal, to take the so-called Western Balkan route, starting in Syria and moving through Turkey, Greece, North Macedonia, Serbia, Austria, Germany, Italy, France and finally the UK. Along the way it will engage local communities, refugees and artists to come together. This will help break down barriers, connect communities and positively influence public attitudes towards people on the move

grantProgramme.title: ACROSS BORDERS: Routes to safety for refugees

data.title: Improving access to mental health services in Kenya
data.description: Kamili will diagnose and treat 12,000 people with mental health issues through existing Kamili clinics and an additional six government nurses and two community health workers, who they will provide with training, work experience and supportive supervision. Nurses will deliver mental health outreach. Kamili will run awareness raising events to reduce stigma, and provide life skills training, savings and loans to beneficiaries, and help them return to their communities after treatment. Kamili will lobby Government to roll out the Kamili community mental health model across Kenya. They will invest in patient management software, to enable easier sharing of mental health data with Government.

grantProgramme.title: Improving Mental Health and Wellbeing in Kenya

data.title: ODI Fellowship Scheme
data.description: ODI are looking to place two junior economists within the Central Banks of Branching Out's focus countries Rwanda, and Zambia on two year secondments with a remit to advancing Financial Inclusion.

grantProgramme.title: Branching Out: Financial Inclusion at the Margins

data.title: Capacity Building for Protection of Girls and Young Women’s Rights in Education and Leadership
data.description: This project will deepen previous activities with in-school Girls Peer Mentoring Clubs, and training and a peer-mentoring programme in Universities alongside training and advocacy work with teachers and other community support structures to build the agency of girls and young women and support the building of a violence free learning environments in institutions of learning,

recipientOrganization.name: MEMPROW: Mentoring and Empowerment Programme for Young Women

data.title: Moving Choose Love from the margins; systemic change to meet a growing crisis
data.description: Help Refugees will build on their existing advocacy work in both the UK, in Europe, Middle East and North Africa (MENA) countries to impact wider systemic change to the refugee crisis in Europe, as well as shift negative public attitudes, through strategic litigation and grassroots advocacy funding. They will also provide small emergency funds to grassroots organisations who are providing front line services to refugees and asylum seekers in European and MENA refugee camps. Working with the organisations they fund, they will enhance the voice of those who have been affected by the refugee crisis in considered media campaigns.

grantProgramme.title: ACROSS BORDERS: Routes to safety for refugees

data.title: The Global Campaign for Mental Health
data.description: We believe in a world where mental health is valued and treated in the same way as physical health. By 2030 everyone, everywhere will have someone to turn to when their mental health needs support. We have established The Global Campaign for Mental Health to be a united global effort to catalyse greater action on global mental health; strong demand for it, more financing, and better frameworks to deliver it.

recipientOrganization.name: The Global Campaign for Mental Health

data.title: Strengthening Leadership and Governance in African Womens Rights Organisations
data.description: Africa Women's Development Fund (AWDF) will continue their work from phase 1 of the Comic Relief grant, this will see 8 women's rights organisations in East and Southern Africa supported to strengthen their governance and organisational capacity and 16 women coached to further their leadership skills. Initially set out as a grant maker, AWDF soon realised that grants cannot be given in isolation, as capacity and leadership building is invaluable in ensuring organisations are sustainable, and have the intended impact. Through this investment, leaders and organisations supported will be more resilient, agile and strategic, and thus able to drive effective change in difficult environments.

data.title: Improving the mental health of perinatal women in Nairobi’s informal settlements
data.description: Women living in Nairobi’s informal settlements (slums) face situations during pregnancy and after birth that put their mental health at risk. Their pregnancy may be unwanted. Lack of partner support, sexual and gender-based violence, and poverty are common. These can lead to maternal anxiety and/or depression and result in poor health for their children. This project will educate communities about common mental health conditions in women during pregnancy and after birth. It will help detect women with these conditions early and refer them to the care and support they need. This will result in better health of women and their babies.

grantProgramme.title: Improving Mental Health and Wellbeing in Kenya

data.title: The Challenge Initiative
data.description: The Challenge Initiative (TCI), is a bold, “business unusual” platform primarily funded for rapidly scaling proven reproductive health and family planning solutions for women and girls living in urban slums. TCI places cities directly in the driver’s seat – by having them contribute their own resources – to implement TCI’s proven approaches, with ongoing technical support and coaching from TCI, to achieve sustainable impact. This project builds on existing support from Comic Relief to expand the work to additional cities in Uganda, Tanzania and Nigeria.

data.title: Protekt Wi Gal Pikin Dem: Addressing sexual violence and discrimination against adolescent girls
data.description: This programme will address multiple & acute forms of violence experienced by girls in & around primary schools Sierra Leone, with a particular focus on Sexual Violence. It will be delivered in three areas: Bo, Kenema & Freetown & will work at multiple levels to address structural violence & gender inequality. It will: strengthen & enforce relevant national laws & regional agreements; deliver a media & advocacy campaign; train statutory service providers, particularly teachers & police; strengthen referral systems & support girls to access justice; establish safe spaces for girls & support them to know & claim their right to a life free from violence; & sensitize communities & families.

data.title: Inclusive Fintech 50: Emerging fintechs for financial inclusion
data.description: Inclusive Fintech 50 (IF50) recognizes promising early-stage fintechs driving financial inclusion. The goal of IF50 is to make these fintechs more visible to investors and to provide the industry with better data, thus promoting greater and more impactful investment in inclusive fintechs that are reaching the un/underbanked.

grantProgramme.title: Branching Out: Financial Inclusion at the Margins

data.title: Bridging Gaps: Innovate for Malaria (B4M)
data.description: Malaria accounts for 38% of all health service visits in Ghana. Through a current project, communities learn to prevent malaria and seek treatment, but also about the health services they are entitled to and the quality of care they should expect. Using methods that foster an honest exchange of ideas between communities and health providers, the project has helped improve local health services. This project will record these experiences so that they can be used to influence communities, Ghana Health Service, parliamentarians and others to change business as usual. The project will push for better health systems and greater resources for malaria leading to better health care for all.

data.title: Haki ya Binti- Phase 2
data.description: This project seeks to address multiple forms of violence against women and girls living in rural areas in three districts in Tanzania (Mpwepwa, Tarime and llemela) by empowering and enabling them to lead social change and mobilising key community actors and local decision-makers to address gender equality, rights, social norms and barriers that face girls through improved local responses. CDF will take over from FORWARD as lead partner in the initiative building on a previous phase of the project in which FORWARD was the lead partner managing this work.

data.title: Evidence based approaches empowering youth with mental health problems to tackle stigma
data.description: Young people in Nairobi face challenges to their mental health. Urban life, changes in the traditional family structure, and poverty can lead to alcohol and drug misuse or other problems. The media portrays people with mental health disorders as violent, mad, or spiritually possessed. Stigma associated with mental health problems is both a cause and an effect of limited access to treatment. This project will replicate Time To Change, a programme that has helped reduce mental health-related stigma in England. It will support young people with experience of mental health problems to talk to members of the public, alongside a campaign to challenge stigma and discrimination in Nairobi.

grantProgramme.title: Improving Mental Health and Wellbeing in Kenya

data.title: Safer Schools for Girls
data.description: Sexual violence in Sierra Leone is widespread, impacting the ability of girls to attend school and advance their education. Plan Sierra Leone and Amazonian Initiative Movement will work to reduce school related gender-based violence against girls in primary schools in the Koinadugu District. The project will take a multi-level approach, focusing on (1) increasing girls/boys understanding of gender-based violence, (2) ensuring schools offer a safer environment for girls, (3) shifting community members attitudes and practices, (4) improving survivors access to services/support, and (5) working with the Government of Sierra Leone to adopt and implement policies that enhances girls’ safety.

data.title: Catalytic financing for Zero Malaria in Mozambique
data.description: The project has three main components:1) Create End Malaria Council and Fund Support to help building political will. A project manager will be recruited to support the implementation of the Fund, and sector-by-sector engagement through trade organisations and Civil Society groups;2) Private sector resource mobilisation, through the design and launch of a Fund. ALMA has conducted mapping of the private sector in Mozambique, and has started to generate financial and in-kind commitments for malaria;3) Map CSOs and identify potential champions to support in-country malaria advocacy and enhance accountability. If a suitable partner is identified, a 1 year sub-grant of 50K will be awarded.

data.title: Creating a women's and girls movement in Malawi that challenge GBV and promotes Women leadership
data.description: Using learning generated through a Comic Relief All In, All Learning grant, GENET (in partnership with CAVWOC and Oxfam Malawi) aim to support 3000 girls & young women to understand their rights and to work with their communities to ensure these rights are upheld. Existing girls & women’s groups in Phalombe & Dowa will be connected to work collectively into the long-term and will raise awareness of gender-related laws and policies, track (and lobby for) resource allocation from district to national level for policy implementation, strengthen community and district structures & processes to uphold girls’ rights and improve access to justice for survivors of gender-based violence & abuse.

data.title: Shifting Norms and Empowering Girls to End Sexual Violence (SNEGES)
data.description: SL is one of the poorest countries globally. 45% of women experience Sexual & Gender Based Violence (SGBV), 39% of girls are married before 18, 13% are married before 15, 88% of girls & women have undergone FGM. RAINBO will work to address these challenges by working with teachers & young people in primary schools in Freetown & Kenema, providing medical & psycho-social support to survivors, strengthening referral pathways, sensitising families & communities to improve their responses to violence & working to strengthen the policy framework at all levels. They will also conduct research to improve understanding of the attitudes which enable violence & to determine what works to end violence.

data.title: Strengthening Mental Health Care and Forensic Psychological Evidence Collection in Kenya
data.description: 47% of women and girls in Kenya have suffered physical or sexual violence, a figure that rises in times of conflict. At least 900 people were sexually violated in the unrest following Kenya’s 2007 national election. Victims faced stigma, a lack of mental health services, and weak police and justice systems. Many crimes were not reported. Cases that made it to court often failed due to lack of robust evidence. PHR Kenya works to improve the collection and use of forensic evidence to better support victims of sexual crimes. This project will extend their work to improve collection of psychological evidence to support legal cases, and help survivors of sexual violence get mental health care.

CSOs will be trained and mobilised to participate in Annual Work Plans and budget-making processes; support to primary health care facilities will be offered to develop, review and disseminate mental health service charters ad community volunteers will use scorecards to monitor services and promote accountability.

data.title: Resilient Action for Inclusive Education (READ)
data.description: This project will work with children and families affected by conflict close to the border of South Sudan. There are a high number of single parent households, children with disabilities and families affected by psychological trauma. Families don't plan for ECD - prioritising primary school instead - but many children (including disabled children) struggle with transition to school and/or drop out early. This project uses a holistic approach including sport and play to create an environment among children, parents and others that is caring, protective and stimulating. As a result, all children will have the chance to achieve their full cognitive, emotional, social and physical potential.

data.title: Strengthening Access, Resources and Transition (StART) using Peer-assisted Supports
data.description: Most children in conflict-affected communities in northern Uganda don't have access to formal pre-school education, despite a national policy being in place. For the last 10 years LABE has been modelling non-formal early childhood development provision using home learning centres. This project aims to strengthen the model, and help school readiness, by using a Child to Child approach where older primary school children and their teachers will support younger children in the transition year at the centres and during the first years of school. As a result, disabled and other vulnerable children are more likely to enrol in school, stay in school, and do well supported by their older peers.

data.title: Support access to inclusive pre-school education by children with disabilities
data.description: This project will work in Amolatar District to improve access to inclusive pre-school education for disabled children. It will also work to ensure retention, learning and transition by these children into primary education supporting their future education prospects. The project will include holistic support including rehabilitation, assistive devices and nutrition to support children to thrive in the pre-school environment and work alongside the district authorities to promote the impact of this being sustained and expanded in future.

data.title: Community Partnership for Early Childhood Development in Moyo District (COPE)
data.description: This project will work in two remote communities in northern Uganda which have some of the worst primary education indicators and where a tiny minority of children have access to early childhood education. The project will establish two model community-led centres for children to play, learn and socialise. These will link to a cluster of other non-formal groups in communities and local primary schools. Parents, community members and local government will be engaged to deliver on government's early childhood development policy. There is a strong focus on nutrition and family learning. As a result of the project, children will have the best possible start to early childhood learning and care.

data.title: Improving access and retention in inclusive education for refugee children with disabilities
data.description: Persons with disabilities are among the most vulnerable refugees in Uganda, and their living conditions are made worse by displacement. Most have fled conflict, war and natural disasters, which also contribute to a higher disability burden among refugees. Among them children with disability are typically hidden, neglected and socially excluded. RLP will work with a range of parents, caregivers, teachers, refugee services and duty bearers to promote the rights of children with disability, and increase their access to education and other support in two zones ? Nakivale, a large refugee settlement in the southwest of Uganda, and in Kampala.

data.description: Reaching Our Goals will better enable marginalised adolescent girls in Dedza, Malawi to make decisions about their future and lead the lives they choose. The project participants, who were selected due to barriers including pregnancy, marriage, and disability, will be supported to complete an accelerated learning programme and transition into mainstream education, vocational training, or employment. Through a netball-based Empowerment Curriculum, girls will have improved capacity to make their own life choices. Delivered to girls and their male peers through netball drills, activities, and games, the Empowerment Curriculum will strengthen girls? sense of self-worth and their value, improve sexual/reproductive health and family planning knowledge, enhance understanding of gender norms, gender-based violence, and how to safely challenge gender stereotypes and negotiate roles in the household and wider community. Participants will be empowered to report gender-based violence and know how to access key services. They will be able to identify their ambitions and the necessary steps to achieve these. Training and induction to Village Savings and Loan groups, cooperatives, entrepreneurship, and income-generating activities will expand girls? knowledge of and access to education, training and work opportunities. Girls and key allies such as headteachers, Mother Groups, and community leaders will be supported to work together to promote marginalised girls? rights and choices. Girls? immediate families (parents, husbands and parents-in-law) will have a broader understanding of suitable activities, including for those who are head of household, married, and have caring responsibilities. Netball tournaments will enhance girls? capacities and community support, while community and district government leaders will develop skills in Sport for Change. Working through established community and government structures, with project participants at the forefront of strategy development and delivery, will bring about longer-term change.

data.title: SafeLives Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 -We are requesting this funding for our work to support victims and survivors of domestic abuse, and frontline professionals during the covid-19 outbreak. Working closely with local and national voluntary sector partners, the DA Commissioner, the national domestic abuse lead for the police and others we are:1. supporting individuals and families who are being asked to self-isolate but who are not safe at home 2. looking after the health and morale of staff and volunteers across the specialist sector 3. sustaining funding for frontline provision and working with funders to set out what the sector needs now. Examples of this to date include: - Extensive on-line information available to victims/survivors of domestic abuse and the professionals supporting them - https://safelives.org.uk/news-views/domestic-abuse-and-covid-19. This has been accessed by over 30,000 thousand individuals and organisations seeking urgent support.- A weekly podcast series giving vital emotional support, reassurance and practical information for DA practitioners, victim/survivors and their families/friends.- Our campaign to encourage friends and neighbours to ?Reach In? to check on anyone they might be worried about - https://safelives.org.uk/reach-in on multiple social media channels. - Our online (free to use) SafeLives Community of DA-focused professionals, which has grown by a staggering 50% in the last month with over 2,200 active members.- Guidance published for children?s social care workers, the police, and other statutory agencies working with families where there is domestic abuse. - We are having regular calls with multiple colleagues in Government including the Home Secretary, Shadow Home Secretary and lead Minister, Victoria Atkins, focusing in particular on encouraging them to create stronger, more comprehensive public awareness campaigns and resource for the response to abuse during this period. We are also supporting Nicole Jacobs (DA Commissioner for England and Wales) and her office, providing her with regular data and practice insights from both professionals and survivors.- We are bringing together a weekly CEOs / service managers call with dozens of frontline voluntary sector leaders. Drawing from that, we?re working on and have already delivered multiple ways of helping services pivot to the new reality successfully. This includes supporting them with the adoption of digital technologies, responding to their calls for new/urgent guidance on specific issues and aspects of abuse and this situation, and providing connection between larger and smaller services who could potentially ?buddy up? or even take part in a more formal mechanism to adopt similar practice to the police ?mutual aid? concept, through which services in different parts of the country can be deployed to each other in times of heightened need and stretch.- We have campaigned for and secured funding and support for frontline services, including £20,000 from a philanthropic foundation (who wish to be anonymous) for 17 of the very smallest ?Leading Lights? accredited services to buy the new kit and equipment they need to do their work remotely. By contrast, the Government has provided just £5,000 to all services across England and Wales for the same purpose.- We have provided advice to employers and service providers such as financial institutions (with Surviving Economic Abuse) to ensure new routes to support are opened up when outside contact for people is so limited.Covid-19 is disproportionately affecting BAME communities. This reflects underlying, deeply rooted structural inequalities. In addition to all of the above, here are some of the ways our approach is both tailored to and reaching BAME communities specifically, and the women and organisations who identify as working specifically on behalf of a Black or minority ethnic community: - Many of the frontline CEOs who are regularly joining our weekly call represent services covering geographic areas with significant BAME populations.- We are joining a regular BAME & DA call to share information/challenges, organised by Meena Kumari of HOPE training and consultancy, and attended by a wide range of organisations including frontline BAME / DA services, academics, and lawyers. It is also attended by Nicole Jacobs, Domestic Abuse Commissioner, and David Lammy MP. Meena is coordinating a joint sector response on BAME communities and domestic abuse to the Home Secretary, and we will be inputting into this.- Our CEO invited Ngozi Fulani from Sistah Space to take part in a dedicated podcast, so she could talk from an authentic perspective about covid challenges specifically as they relate to Black women of African and Caribbean heritage. We hope this will be followed by a similar podcast with Ikwro, who work specifically with women who form part of the UK?s Middle Eastern diaspora (as our CEO does herself).- We are collaborating with Jasvinder Sanghera from Karma Nirvana on work to support people at risk of or experiencing ?honour? based violence, FGM and forced marriage. This will include guidance for BAME communities with a specific focus on these issues, and a piece of guidance for those working in education. Karma Nirvana have highlighted to us that these aspects of DA are not getting enough recognition by Government or the media despite evidence of increasing need. We are keen to support their messages.- Much of our online content and guidance is survivor led, and we are planning bespoke content with SafeLives Pioneer Naomi Donald, exploring the impact of domestic abuse on young black women during covid and what suitable and effective responses should be. - We have used our social media platforms to showcase and promote the needs and specialisms of BAME-led charities, persistently championing the need for the smallest and most specialist organisations to be properly recognised and supported in this period and more generally.- We are working with BAME specialist organisations to shape materials in our Reach In campaign ? to ensure the campaign resonates with and works for survivors from a range of different communities. - When approached bilaterally by colleagues at the Lottery to write proposals for short-term support for national organisations, we quickly brought Imkaan into the conversation and ensured the needs of their organisation and members were fully represented in the resulting paper (To note, this paper is with NLCF England for imminent decision. The proposals contained within it will ? we hope ? be supported at a programmatic level by Social Finance. You have received an application from them which describes the important strategic and analytical role they would play if funding is approved).Though not asked about above, it?s also valuable to note that we?re working closely with Stay Safe East on the specific risks and experiences of disabled women during this period. Many are likely to be shielding or in other constrained situations, and SSE have reported increased instances of, for example, medications being withheld, and financial control being tightened. We?re also helping to promote the work of Sisters of Frida, who have highlighted the need for a proper response for disabled women at this time. Covid-19 has meant we have had to cancel or postpone all our training and consultancy / advisory work until the current crisis has been resolved, with a net loss of £125k per month, potentially over the next 10 months. This represents a loss of up to £1.25m. This would usually have subsidised core posts which are hard to fundraise for from statutory or voluntary funders but which are critical to our current response.

Sorani, Luganda, Mandarin, Mandinka, Mirpuri, Ndebele, Pashto, Potwari, Punjabi, Romani, Romanian, Russian, Rutooro, Shona, Sindhi, Slovak, Somali, Swahili, Taita, Tigrinya, Tumbuka, Turkish, Urdu, Vietnamese, West African creoles, Wolof, Yoruba.) Sessional workers will encourage service user take up and consistent engagement.Daughters who are 12+ and young mothers will be supported by an experienced youth counsellor. All service users with children under 18 will be supported to find solutions to parenting problems by sessional workers in conjunction with childcare services, Safeguarding Officer, and youth counsellors.This work will support 120 women and 240 children at high risk (based on an average of 2 children per woman).Sessional workers and counsellors will be supported and supervised by the Safeguarding Officer, qualified and experienced in managing case work and counselling services. With them and with existing case workers and childcare staff (as appropriate) risk will be removed and reduced, referring cases to social work and police as necessary. Project staff will also liaise with health visitors, midwives, GPs, and other partners to ensure best possible outcomes for women and children.Counsellors will receive regular external group supervision according to best practise.The Safeguarding Officer will be line-managed by our CEO who is line-managed by the Board of Directors. data.title: Scottish Association for Mental Health Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 -See Me is Scotland?s national programme to end mental health stigma and discrimination. The See Me programme is at the forefront of efforts to eliminate mental health stigma and discrimination. Our vision is to end mental health stigma and discrimination, enabling people who experience mental health problems to live fulfilled lives. We work towards our vision through facilitating cultural and behavioural change in education and the wider youth sector, workplaces, health & social care, and communities. We apply a range of approaches to achieve change including: social movement, capacity building, campaigns and policy activities. Social contact is central to all that we do and through empowering adult and youth volunteers we ensure that improvement and change is directly influenced by people with lived experience. Prior to the Covid 19 pandemic mental health stigma and discrimination continued to blight the lives of substantial sections of society. A summary of impact is available on pages 5 and 6 of See Me?s 3 Year Evaluation report (https://seemescotland.org/media/9723/sm-cross-cutting.pdf), which was published in the weeks before the COVID-19 lockdown. The COVID-19 pandemic has dramatically increased the conditions which can cause psychological distress with many experts predicting an emerging mental health crisis (see NOTES). Although the full impact of the pandemic in relation to mental health stigma and discrimination has yet to be defined; our experience, the early data and research suggests that the level of both stigma and discrimination will increase and will not be experienced uniformly. Many people will continue to struggle to reach out and access the support they require due to stigma (public, self, by association and structural); attitudes, prejudice and actions of people across a range of settings will continue to prevent people with mental health problems and illness achieving the outcomes they seek. This will be exacerbated by intersectionality and the likelihood of inequalities experienced by people with mental health problems and mental illness will be heightened with the most vulnerable suffering the most. The need to extend action to tackle mental health stigma and discrimination has never been greater. Within this context, it is key for See Me to empower more people to take action.For obvious reasons, physical distancing around COVID has led to an increase in demand for telephone consultancy support and guidance, online delivery including tools for engagement, training and digital resources, and an overall rise in online communications and digital output. This increase in demand highlights the urgent need for an enhanced suite of online resources and tools. See Me?s current funding will not cover all of the costs involved in the digitalisation and online publishing of the resources required to meet increasing stakeholder expectations and need. With this in mind, we would use the funding in the following areas:1. Fast tracking the development and publishing of digital tools, content and online support for workplaces. We are already struggling to meet rising interest and demand from workplaces and predict this will increase over the coming months. As people begin to return to work, with easing of lockdown restrictions, addressing stigma will be an essential element of workplace mental health. Our focus on leadership, inclusive cultures and practice and on building confidence in responding to and speaking out about mental health is of increasing interest; many of the outputs we have, if digitalised and made available online, will be of particular value to more workplaces. Additional funding would enable us to act swiftly to respond to greater levels of interest and demand. We would enhance the resources available on our online platform, providing a wider range of tools, supports and self-service / Do It Yourself options for employers, managers and employees to take forward action to address stigma, with limited involvement of the See Me team. In addition once the enhancements to the online resources are made we would ensure we proactively target and engage specific employers, sectors and industries to reach priority groups. 2. Extending our communications to engage and encourage action to address stigma in priority populations and groups most affected/ disengaged by COVID. As the national anti stigma programme we have increased our communications output (media; online; social media) to ensure a specific focus on stigma and discrimination within the context of addressing mental health and wellbeing issues, arising from COVID. We produced an immediate response following lockdown, tailoring our messages to have a particular emphasis on stigma, normalising mental health and mental health challenges at this time, promoting the importance of reaching out, of listening to and supporting friends and family and of reaching out to others to get help. We quickly reintroduced digital campaigns including It?s OK, Pass the Badge and feels FM to encourage social contact and online conversations about mental health. We supported volunteers to identify and create different ways of engaging people to share experiences, raise awareness of stigma and discrimination and promote continued action through the use of online and non contact solutions. Most of this activity was based on universal messaging towards the general adult/ children and young people populations. Additional resource would enable us to work with more of our partners, specific volunteers and community champions to adapt and where necessary create focused, targeted communications for specific priority groups of the community (those less likely or able to be engaged). This would include extension of our current BAME social movement project in Glasgow. We would be happy to provide a breakdown of these costs.NOTES1. Selection of current findings and ongoing research:Mental Health Foundation, data from a diverse Citizens? Jury - https://www.mentalhealth.org.uk/our-work/research/coronavirus-mental-health-pandemic/covid-19-inequality-briefingLockdown Lowdown, views of young people -https://www.youthlinkscotland.org/media/4534/lockdownlowdown-results-by-demographic-breakdown.pdfJournal discussion on psychological factors during pandemics and evidence of these from China -https://academic.oup.com/qjmed/article/113/5/311/5813733There is ongoing research to understand the effects of the pandemic on mental health in the UK & Scotland:Mental Health Foundation - https://www.mentalhealth.org.uk/our-work/research/coronavirus-mental-health-pandemic/aboutSAMH - https://www.samh.org.uk/about-us/news-and-blogs/study-launched-to-understand-mental-health-implications-of-covid-19

data.title: Expansion of LGBTI+ project
data.description: COVID19 - We are requesting funding 1. To allow us to extend the contract to one of our LGBT+ staff to cope with increased work load and current COVID 19 situation. 2. To purchase 1 laptop3. To Purchase 3 mobile phones and mobile/Wi-Fi vouchers 4. To purchase basic clothing 5. To purchase food and or food vouchers6. Travel costs for clients struggling financially and or at higher risk1 (funding to extend the current staff contract) ? help us meet the increased referrals of women experiencing domestic abuse. There has been a high increase in women with no recourse to public funds, some of them are thrown out of the house by their partners.Shakti?s Maitri project (LGBTI+ is funded by Comic Relief (tampon tax fund) the project supports BME LGBT+ and also outreach women. Initially we applied for one full time staff. There were delays in appointing the staff due to not finding the suitable person for the post. It was crucial for us to appoint a suitable person with right attitude and beliefs about sexuality to deliver the service to BME LGBT+ persons, therefore we were over cautious in recruiting. Therefore, it took us 7 months to have someone in the post. Shakti was successful in negotiating with Comic Relief to use the surplus from year 1 funding to appoint a part time until June 2020 post to kick start the project ? this has worked to the project?s advantage.We now realise that we underestimated the potential demand and resources we needed for the project. The project receives referrals from other cities in Scotland and is currently supporting referrals from Edinburgh, Stirling, Dundee and Glasgow. Although the numbers of LGBT+ person are small they are spread across Scotland, therefore takes the staff lot more time to support them ( travel time and also multi agency work is more complicated). The staff also support women fleeing domestic abuse who are living with the perpetrators.We have agencies from Aberdeen and Fife enquiring about the support we can offer to the BME LGBT+ persons. Supporting LGBT+ service users/referrals was difficult due to the confidentiality and risk to the persons, and this has been exacerbated by the COVID 19. COVID 19 has put breaks to our planned work, the project staff are unable to do the awareness raising work as well as struggling to support the LGBT+ clients who are placed in cities out with Edinburgh and or living with their families as well as dealing with the increase in new referrals.Not having the appropriate and most needed support will put these women/persons at higher risk and they may potentially lose trust in any agencies in future. Therefore, it is vital to the well-being of the BME LGBT+ persons and women who are living with the perpetrators that we continue to offer the current level of support.2 and 3 (laptop, mobiles/Wi-Fi and Vouchers)Due to lockdown and the safety of its staff and service users, Shakti stopped face to face support and is contacting its service users using technology (virtual meetings/chats), however not all service users have access to laptops and or smart phones, therefore creating a barrier in reaching to them, causing distress and frustration to both the service users and the staff. Some of the service users are young people or women with no recourse to public funds and or on very low income. Therefore we would like to purchase one laptop, mobiles and vouchers)4 and 5 (Basic clothing and food)Most of our service users are struggling with food purchase. We are receiving food from local food banks but some of the food available doesn?t meet the cultural/religious food requirements of our clients like vegetarian and halal food. With the funds received from CR we will buy appropriate food or food vouchers. We have women and their children (if any) leaving their homes with nothing and needing basic clothing and toiletries, especially this is so much difficult for women with no recourse to public funds.6 (travel)As mention above women with children and single women/ young girls are struggling with their finances and travelling to buy food and other essentials is expensive, especially when you have children; also when the lockdown rules are relaxed, we are planning to start our face to face meetings. It will be beneficial to the young persons, if we could pay their travel expenses to attend group activities. The project started a young women?s group, just now not specific to LGBT+ but the idea behind the group is to gradually build it to be specific to BAME LGBT+. What the staff have realised is that the LGBT+ they are supporting have multiple added risks compared to non LGBT+ BAME persons. This is an example to illustrate some of the challenges the staff are facing due to COVID 19The staff is supporting a young Trans person who is living with her/his mum. Due to lockdown mum allowed dad back into her home and as a result the young person got unwell and suicidal. The perpetrator is a stepdad to the young person and has been very abusive (sexually abused) towards her/him. Mother is not a protective factor in this young person?s life; she is a strict Muslim, encouraging the child to forget about the sexual abuse and doesn?t support the young person. The young person is not looked after by her/his mum ? no proper clothes and hygiene, lacks confidence. The COVID 19 has made things worse for the young person and the support she/he was receiving from us and the school. Our staff referred the young person to social work to get support, after nearly 4 weeks the social worker got back to our worker. They arranged to have a meeting with the mother and the child to discuss the safety of mother (not acknowledging the abuse suffered by the young person). Our young person requested the social worker to invite our staff to the virtual meeting but social work ignored the request. It is our staff the young person trusts and has been open with about her/his problems but still social worker seem to ignore the request. This is one of the challenges our staff face when statutory agencies undermine the support and views given by the third sector. In this difficult times the young person has only one support line which is our staff. Our staff did a very good job with the young person and continues to support her/him. The school are involved in this case but it is closed now. There is lot more to this case which I can discuss it with you in detail if you wish to.

data.title: Social Bite Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -We are seeking funding towards the production and distribution of 2,000 emergency food packs that we plan to deliver each weekday to people who are most likely to be at risk of limited access to food or cooking facilities in Scotland in July and August.
 
 As you will read below, we have been providing this service on a much larger scale since 20th March. Our original aim was to support people most at risk during the Covid-19 crisis, who due to being homeless or experiencing food poverty, would struggle to access sufficient food and equally to stay at home and/or self-isolate. 
 
 Our campaign to date has focussed particularly on people affected by homelessness who in some cases did not have any shelter, sources of food and/or no access to cooking facilities. We have also targeted our support to children and families most at risk of having insufficient food during the crisis with a particular focus on children in poverty who in normal circumstances would be receiving free school meals.
 
 We are now planning proactively for the next phase of the crisis, when lockdown restrictions are eased but where particular groups will still be at heightened risk of having no food or no cooking facilities or where people will suddenly be experiencing increased financial hardship as a result of redundancy / loss of income. We anticipate the most at-risk groups to be people affected by homelessness who are still being accommodated in emergency settings with no cooking facilities as well as children and families affected by ?holiday hunger?. We are anticipating that an increased number of children will be at risk of hunger during the summer holidays on the back of the current crisis with many families being tipped into food poverty due to redundancy / loss of income or who are waiting to access benefits (in Scotland, school summer holidays run from beginning of July to mid-August). 
 
 We are working with our 97 charity partners to understand where the greatest need will be post-lockdown, to ensure that our lifeline to these individuals and families is not suddenly dropped with no other food provision support structure in place. Based on our assessment to date, we plan to target deliveries in July and August to 2,000 people each weekday across Edinburgh and the Lothians, Glasgow and Aberdeen.

data.title: Social Finance Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -Context. 
 
 Domestic abuse leaves vulnerable people, including children, living in fear in the very place where they should feel most safe and secure ? inside their own home. We have watched a wave of countries whose lockdown was further ahead see a rise in their reported domestic abuse and other forms of violence/abuse against women and children. That pattern is being replicated in the UK where indicators suggest a rise in both the severity in pre-existing abusive situations, and risk of new patterns of abusive behaviour. This is due to a reduction in inhibiting factors and safeguards which is also exacerbated by pre-existing inequalities for many with protected characteristics. 
 
 Emergency funds from government and grant-making trusts are currently being directed to support frontline domestic abuse charities to meet these challenges and directly support those that need it the most. This will help respond to the increase in needs and mitigate the dramatic and instantaneous fall many charities in have faced in their income but will not be enough. For instance, funding recently announced by the Government for the specialist VAWG sector will be split across a range of social issues and crime types, from rape to modern slavery.
 
 A national effort is needed to support and enhance the frontline response, in order to 
 i) understand cumulative need across the UK, 
 ii) provide coordination and secure solutions to fill identified gaps in knowledge, capacity and capability, 
 iii) communicate to multiple audiences in a way that mobilises as many people and as much resource as possible and 
 iv) maximise the likelihood of an effective and sustainable legacy beyond this emergency response with stronger, better foundations for future. 
 
 A group of national domestic abuse charities (including our Drive partners, SafeLives and Respect) have agreed to jointly work towards these goals over the next six months. Each organisation brings deep connections to frontline organisations, victims and survivors. This group of charities have asked us to take on a coordination role given our existing links to the sector, enabling them to focus their scarce resources to frontline work.
 
 Objectives and activities
 
 The funding from Comic Relief will enable us to go beyond our current coordination role and proactively support these efforts ? acting as independent facilitator and broker with this group of charities. Those organisations range from the large to the very tiny, and we will play a programmatic role, giving shape to the work of nine organisations all of whom are working at full tilt and will benefit from the ?glue? that brings all their distinct activities into a set of work that achieves more than the sum of its parts. 
 
 This will build on the role Social Finance has played with Drive partners and other cross-sector partnerships beyond domestic abuse, maximising our added value over the next six months.
 
 More specifically, we anticipate the funding will help:
 
 1. Rapidly aggregating real-time data and insights (e.g. building on the dynamic surveys these national organisations have conducted with frontline organisations since the onset of the covid-19 crisis and lockdown period), understanding the needs as well as positive changes that have been created during this period and should be continued,
 2. Feeding those insights straight back into the emergency responses to enable rapid feedback and adjustment (local frontline, response of the Government and key statutory agencies) to reduce the risks from abuse in the next six months; as well as to the Domestic Abuse Commissioner?s office, keeping information and decisions flowing between all parties. 
 3. Identifying systemic gaps to inform the strategy needed once lockdown and other crisis measures are removed, and developing opportunities to respond to those gaps, brokering necessary partnerships and shaping action plans around these.
 
 This will involve a rapid programme of interviewing and sharing, analysis and synthesis as well as workshops bringing together national domestic abuse charities, statutory services and others. It will also be informed by other sectors? responses to Covid-19 (for example, mental health services) as well as statutory bodies such as the police, social services and the criminal justice system, and private organisations such as financial institutions.
 
 We will work to make this near-term programme of work the springboard for a longer-term set of relationships and approach. We want this to be a genuinely collective effort, with proper thought given to how we achieve an inclusive and representative impact. Our hope is that we can make an important contribution during this national emergency and to the future we build afterward.

data.title: Somerset and Avon Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -We have three main areas of work that require funding during this period and which we hope could be supported through the Recovery Grant: 
 1. Additional staff capacity and support required to transition to new ways of working remotely (£9,050)
 
 This includes:
 - Increased clinical supervision for all staff and frontline volunteers. 
 - An online resilience training package for all staff and volunteers. 
 - Additional management time over this period ? the Management Team have been required to work extra paid hours over the transition to remote working as we worked tirelessly to move our systems and set up new processes and procedures plus offer increase support to our teams. 
 
 2. A new Web Chat facility 
 
 We are requesting £20k towards the design, development, and implementation of a new, bespoke Web Chat service for victim-survivors of sexual abuse across the Avon and Somerset region. This secure, instant service will be available to anyone over the age of 13 regardless of gender, status, situation, or background. Web Chat will allow us to provide ?listening?, support, signposting, and referral into services for groups who are struggling to access our helpline during lockdown, as well as groups traditionally not served well by helplines. Web Chat offers a new way of communicating with victim-survivors of rape and sexual abuse both during Covid-19 lockdown measures and beyond. 
 
 As part of the design, development, and delivery we will be: 
 - Accessing professional/technical support to select the right product for our needs with the support of DOT PROJECT. DOT PROJECT will provide light touch support to: 
 o Understand the needs of users: User research to document the immediate and long-term requirement of those who will use it and those who will manage it (SARSAS staff and volunteers) 
 o Creating clear requirements for the Web Chat tool: based on the findings of the user research DOR PROJECT will create clear requirements to inform the functionalities required within the Web Chat tool
 o Support the identification of digital partners to implement the Web Chat Function: DOR PROJECT will aim to work with a digital expert who has experience in implementing a Web Chat function. We will liaise with the Tch vs Abuse digital experts to bring in learning from these projects. 
 
 - Purchasing the technology and testing the new system 
 
 - Funding increased staff and volunteer time in the development and implementation phase plus the initial months of delivering the new service and supervision of the volunteer teams. 
 
 3. Lost income because of Covid
 
 We have lost income because of Covid-19 that could destabilise our financial resilience and have a devastating impact on our (already stretched) reserves position. 
 
 We are seeking £11k towards lost income because of Covid-19 (described in more detail in 2.2 below). This includes: 
 - £6k in lost rental income from our Taunton office 
 - £5k decrease in unrestricted raised income.
