data.title: Southall Black Sisters Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 - Changes to the way we streamline referrals: After the lockdown was announced, the SBS helpline began to receive calls from women expressing fears for their safety due to the government guidance for families to stay at home. One caller told us: ?I don't know how long this situation with the virus will last but I'm sure that it's going to be difficult and very stressful for us. It is not obvious and tricky, the gaslighting and the crazy making... my hands are shaking and I can't stop it! I need your help and your experience to make this self-isolation bearable.? Another existing user called in panic as her partner?s actions were putting her at risk ?We are separated but he refuses to move out. It was okay before because he would be out until late, but the Covid pandemic is causing more upset, but I have no control over him. He chooses when he wants to go out, putting my children and I at risk of catching the virus. He went out drinking recently, then came home and called me names in front of my child. I?m trying to shield my children from it but I can?t. I?ve pleaded with him to go and stay with his family or friends, I told him not to drink at home but he does what he wants, it?s a control thing. I feel depressed, alone, I?m having to negotiate with him when I don?t want to, and I don?t know when he?s going to retaliate.? In a matter of days, the helpline has become the main source of referrals due to walk-in services being suspended. We are trying to fundraise for staff costs to ensure that the helpline can operate for additional hours to meet the increase in demand. We would like to invest in increasing helpline staff capacity to ensure we are responding to all calls promptly and not leaving users waiting for prolonged periods (given this may be their only chance to speak safely, we have to maximise our capacity to respond to each and every call). 
 - Changes to casework: Within days of lockdown being announced, SBS invested considerably in IT resources (upgrading our software and hardware system which could not support home working of all our staff) and purchase laptops, printers, scanners and other IT equipment for all frontline staff. Some expensive software such as call handling and Microsoft Team was essential to effectively supervise newly recruited staff and ensure coordinated teamwork but the unexpected expenses have caused severe strain on our finances. 
 In terms of challenges in undertaking casework remotely, it is taking our advocates significantly longer to contact and engage social services and local authority housing departments. In the absence of face-to-face appointments, we have to spend more time trying to make contact online and by phone. Even when our advocates manage to make contact, the process of engagement and resolution of a matter takes much longer. Whereas previously it might have taken two days of physical attendance at social services offices to resolve a matter, vulnerable women and children are now left in conditions of destitution and at serious risk for longer periods of time. From our initial analysis we have noted a sharp rise in demand among existing users (40% rise in calls and emails) and a 12% increase in new referrals. As a result, we have had to undertake an increased amount of intense advocacy work over the phone or online. This means that each engagement with users takes longer than usual in respect of taking statements, gathering evidence and providing much needed legal and other support. We have suspended our volunteer programme (due to difficulties ensuring proper supervision and user safeguarding concerns)- this has meant more pressure on staff who have had to take on the additional responsibilities. Staff are also conducting additional welfare checks on our most vulnerable users twice a week. All these additional measures mean that staff hours and costs have risen considerably. On top of increase in work hours, frontline staff continue to meet our particularly vulnerable, high risk clients face to face to support in completing and signing urgent documents for court hearings, for obtaining welfare support, and with travelling to alternative accommodation. Many also need to rely on our IT resources to engage in essential court hearings or appointments via video link. Migrant women who are destitute continue to rely on us to physically deliver food and other necessities and/or make subsistence payments to them on a weekly basis. We are desperately trying to fundraise to meet the rising cost of cleaning of our premises and the cost of sanitisers, tissues and PPEs without which staff undertaking physical contact are placed at risk. 
 - Increased counselling support: This is one area of work which we have had to rapidly and constantly expand as both existing and new users are reaching out with increased anxiety and panic around Covid-19. In addition to increasing counselling on substantive issues of trauma and abuse from 1.5 days to 4 days a week, we have had to initiate a 30-minute Covid-19 crisis counselling for users particularly affected by the pandemic. We are constantly inundated with demand and need to continue to fundraise to pay the additional costs of the counsellor. 
 - Remote outreach and virtual support group: From early April, SBS moved its support group online via Whatsapp and increased it to an additional day. Shortly after, from April 20th we commenced outreach surgeries online, with live streaming on social media and rights-based Q&As. With the help of the London Community Fund, we purchased data plans for users to help connect them remotely. However, as weeks are progressing women are reporting privacy and safety concerns and are requesting more secure connections and advanced technology. They are also requesting to see each other as many are not good at typing complex thoughts and sentences in English and would prefer to say their thoughts aloud in a shared safe space, supported by friends. For many living alone, the interaction with the support group is the only conversation in their day, so in addition to the Whatsapp groups, they are desperately seeking an opportunity to interact face to face. Others reported they are ?vision learners? and would only be able to learn and participate in support group activities if they could see and learn. Women are also worried about falling behind their ESOL and other training workshops/classes and want to recommence these online. Funding permitting, SBS would like to purchase tablets/iPads for the support group and install secure video conferencing technology. We also need to train the women in navigating the technology safely. To continue women?s? learning we would like to expand to conducting online classes which equip women with essential skills but also amplify and raise Women?s Voices so that they are not silenced by this lockdown and pandemic. 
 - Emergency accommodation: The MHCLG have said they cannot support abused women who need safe accommodation, without first carrying out surveys to assess levels of demand. Unfortunately, the ensuing crisis demands more urgent interim measures which are not being put in place. Even prior to the pandemic, refuges were already unable to cope with current levels of demand. For example, in 2018-19, 64% of referrals to England refuges were declined. In the same year, only 5% of refuge vacancies listed could accommodate women with NRPF . The situation has been rendered much worse due to the Covid-19 crisis. Due to increased demand and due to lockdown related closures, availability of safe bed spaces has critically dried up. At March end for instance, there was only 1 bed available in refuge accommodation in the whole of Wales. When our advocacy manager mapped available spaces in our catchment area, she reported a 45% decline in availability. Many refuges suspended new referrals within the first two weeks of the lockdown due to the need to isolate and safeguard other residents or because of the lack of ?move-on? accommodation or due to staff illnesses. SBS already administers an England wide NRF fund to pay for accommodation and subsistence costs for women and children with NRPF but due to increased demand and inability to move on existing users, this fund is falling short of meeting the rising need. We urgently need crisis housing funds for women with NRPF both to meet needs of new referral clients but also to extend the tenancies for existing NRPF clients who cannot move on at this time (comprising about 60% of our user base). 
 Our modified way of working has already received good feedback and positive reports from service users:
 ?I just want to say big THANK YOU to SBS things you all doing for US as an organization. Taking care of us in every way. Keeping support group on line version, something we look forward to every week. Helping with food delivering to our door step it's massive thing Suman, also money I got from SBS, I ask only £20 for my telephone bill. But I got £200. It's so supportive and huge help, after all I felt little bit of happiness, because I got someone. I know them help me whenever I need help, I felt safe, it helping my mental well-being. The Emotional support you always giving us?.
 
 ?I feel more depressed because I have to spend the whole day in my home. I feel more depressed because of the uncertainty and I am worried about what will happen about my visa and immigration situation. I want to work again like before in a nursing home so I am very anxious about the future. I find the SBS support group and counselling very helpful especially when I share with the counsellor, I feel more relaxed after talking to her?. 
 
 ?I think SBS are doing incredible work and checking in on us even now. I am sometimes overwhelmed by my situation and I had a court hearing last week which did not go well (It was telephone and due to covid the judge was not prepared). I also have no contact with my children now due to the Covid situation ? although it is allowed but because I am in shared accommodation, I cannot see my children (also their dad was aggressive and opposing stuff). I also feel overwhelmed at not being able to be there to support my children and this is impacting on my relationship with them?. 
 
 ?As I have sensitive health, I am really scared of this Covid Pandemic. When I heard about the lockdown I because so hopeless and I was thinking how I am going to survive. I see people stock piling food, I didn?t want to do but at least I wanted to buy for a week but I didn?t have enough money. My anxiety hit me hard. But before lockdown SBS gave me weekly subsistence and some food and said they will look after us even in the lockdown then my anxiety calmed down and I felt relaxed. I am so thankful to SBS supporting me along with all the situations. I am amazed and happy to join the WhatsApp group which makes me feel I am not abandoned. We can support each other, share our ideas and be mentally strong through this. I appreciate and thank you so much SBS for supporting us during this pandemic.?

data.title: Spina Bifida Hydrocephalus Scotland (SBH Scotland) Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -Spina bifida is a developmental disorder that arises in 1 in 1000 pregnancies. The physical symptoms are paralysis from the waist down (requiring lifetime use of a wheelchair) and bowel and bladder dysfunction. 80% of those with spina bifida are also affected by hydrocephalus which may lead to problems with cognitive development. Infants born with the disability will require life-long support and have mutiple complex support needs. Founded in 1965, SBH Scotland provides a life time commitment of holistic family support to over 4000 individuals affected in Scotland. 
 The families and children we work with deal with numerous daily challenges because of the disabilities, and now are terrified at what Covid-19 will bring for their health, wellbeing and financial situation. We have handled over 2500 contacts in April from our service users who are looking for reassurance and advice, especially as many are at high risk due to complex comorbidities. 
 
 In summary, we have identified the following New Covid-19 needs from the families we support ;
 - Health - Our service users have regular hospital appointments to monitor and treat conditions including pressure sores, bladder/bowel issues. Routine health appointments are being cancelled and NHS reactions to emergency situations delayed. The mobility of many children are being affected, possibly with long term consequences. 
 Examples;
 ? A family dealing with over a month?s delay for what would normally be an emergency neurosurgery procedure and family seeing marked deterioration in a child?s mobility which could be permanent if further nerve damage occurs
 ? A likely fracture (susceptibility is because of paralysis caused by SB) that is being managed conservatively at home as the visiting medic (fully gowned) deemed a hospital visit too high risk for the individual. As such they have had to take decision that long term implications of an untreated fracture is preferable to exposure to Covid-19
 ? Anxiety re having to go to a new clinic to undergo a necessary bladder management procedure given risks of Covid-19, but facing risk of kidney scarring if they don?t go to the clinic
 ? A child having to have orthoses fitted by an untrained person via phone guidance as the risk deemed too high to attend the hospital. The orthoses don?t fit and the child?s mobility is severely impacted
 - Mental health- There is a high incidence of depression among the population we support. Covid-19 is adding additional vulnerabilities to their mental health especially now for families having to manage all care without any respite. This is impacting emotional and physical wellbeing. 
 Example
 ? A family not having access to their usual respite and needing support to source alternative means, including SBH Scotland vouching for them to apply for exceptions to rules in order to access respite where significant family breakdown is indicated
 - Financial- The individuals we support usually have low income and many are already on the poverty line. There is concern regarding increased household costs of food, heating, lighting etc. with schools shut. 
 - Medical supplies- There is a concern regarding accessing medical supplies and daily care packages care. There is a particular concern for adult service users who are now self-isolating/or their elderly carers are self-isolating and they are unable to pick up prescriptions. 
 - Isolation- Many of our families are now facing total isolation as they are shielding to protect their child with spina bifida/hydrocephalus as many have complex health conditions. The wider team in the community do not have the skills and expertise to provide the support they need and also understand their anxieties. We are witnessing a rise in emotional problems for those families that have now be isolated for over 6 weeks with no end in sight.
 Example;
 ? For our wheelchair users problems have occurred where food packages have been left on the door step. 
 - Safeguarding- We have had calls from education, health and social care professionals who are now relying on our support staff to keep in contact with vulnerable families who may fall off the radar due to school and community centre closures. With enforced isolation there is increased risk for vulnerable families For example, we support many families experiencing issues including; child protection, domestic abuse, homelessness, poor housing, poor finances, domestic abuse and substance misuse. 
 The Family Support team at SBH Scotland have replaced regular home visits , clinics and group work with a range of services to help address these new Covid-19 related needs . Our support services are delivered by the equivalent of 8 full time Support Workers . Services are delivered across Scotland via West, North and East Regional teams.
 The additional funding received from Comic Relief will contribute towards the running costs of SBH Scotland?s family support and specialist clinical support service, plus associated core organisational costs . Full details of the Covid-19 Services we are now delivering are outlined in the next question.

data.title: Women's Voices on VAOW phase 2 ? Communication Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -We are applying for funding which will enable us to build our communications capacity so that we can continue to reach out to victims of domestic and sexual violence during the COVID-19 pandemic. The current situation has led us to recognise the vital need for improved communication systems in order to be visible and accessible to women in our community, using new forms of technology. We see this as an investment to enhance the ways we are able to continue working locally during the COVID19 restrictions, over the long recovery period following, and beyond.
 
 Since April, our referrals have increased by over 40% compared to the same period last year. As a local Violence Against Women and Girls charity, we have been able to keep our 24 Hour Help Line going during lock down. However, we have encountered problems with its technical capacity (currently it sits on one telephone line and is being diverted to staff who are home working) which has resulted in us being unable to divert the helpline to certain phones reducing its availability. In addition, if the line is busy callers are unable to leave a message. Increasingly, women are contacting us via email or social media channels as our Help Line is busy, or because this is the safest way for them to contact us. However, we have recognised that we do not have the capability or capacity to respond to service users effectively using these channels at present. 
 
 Our request for funding is to enable our Help Line system, social media channels and website to be improved technologically so that we can meet the changing needs of women in our community, and build our accessibility to reach out to our potential and current service users in a variety of ways during this crisis, and beyond.

Social distancing and isolation have made it impossible to deliver our face to face work in secondary schools, and to parents and health professionals. As such stem4 recognises that we will need to work differently to maintain service provision and expand our reach to those most in need.With this in mind, we would like to increase and expand pupil access through extended market penetration to reach new student communities and envisage this being carried out through the following activities:a. Appointment of an Education Co-ordinator who can further expand the current links we have with schools both regionally and nationally, along with forging links with colleges and universities where there is most needb. Continue to target schools with a high pupil premium but additionally to further reach schools where there is a higher prevalence of BAME communities particularly in London and the South Eastc. Tailor our conference content and delivery to include: The effects and signs of increased mental ill health impacted by uncertainty, increased anxiety, loneliness, bereavement and a lack of access to services etc. as a direct consequence of COVID- 19 ? Promotion of enhanced emotional resilience in general and also in response to the impact of COVID-19 ? A focus on reducing potential discrimination through health status and culture? Enhancing community connection and positivity whilst accommodating social distancing? Promote positive role models via BAME stem4 ambassadorsd. Deliver co-collaborative workshops (respecting social distancing measures) to carry out ethnographic research with young people to obtain feedback on impact and resources, with a particular focus to include members of BAME communities e. Culturally and linguistically tailor our COVID-19 related resources through translation into two of the most common languages widely spoken in the first instance in BAME communities e.g. Urdu and Bengali f. Increase our focus on the launch of Head Ed Digital and Head Ed Bite Size (self-guided on-line learning specifically developed for COVID-19 during home school learning)g. Maximise the uptake of our current apps. In addition, our new app Move Mood (launch end May) will be especially relevant since the rise in depression in young people and adults will be high as a direct consequence of COVID-19 and more widely young people will benefit from the motivating element of the app h. Broaden our marketing strategy ? in addition to website and social media, we need to explore other appropriate platforms to increase access and participation i. Evaluate the effectiveness of our extended resources through a small research project/survey using the findings to create a good practice framework to inform delivery of similar activities in other parts of the UK in both short and longer termk. Evaluate and action further adaptation of our apps where there is distinct need l. Appointment of a part time Project Manager (6 months in first instance) to manage the increased burden on staff and existing planned project delivery. The toll of new COVID-19 specific projects, new resource creation and the associated Marketing, PR and Fundraising responses has placed significant demand on respective roles. This role would enable stem4 to fulfil all demands. data.title: STT Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 -STT is requesting Covid-19 Emergency funding from Comic Relief in order to maintain our increased delivery of community campaigns. This is crucial in positively impacting vulnerable communities, including minority ethnic communities, and disrupting modern slavery and human trafficking (MSHT). Comic Relief is a valued partner of STT, having worked together from STT?s inception in 2005 to more recently granting our work with Syrian refugees in Greece and Turkey as part of Across Borders. We are so grateful for the support of Comic Relief in all that it has enabled STT to do. We now ask for additional funding to allow STT to continue to meet the need for our service, which we will detail in this application. Founded in 2006 to coincide with the bicentenary of the abolition of the slave trade, STOP THE TRAFFIK developed its intelligence-led approach to trafficking prevention in 2015. With support from IBM and Facebook, we were able to expand our reach, informing our focus at a local, national and global level. Our solutions are grounded in people, technology and collaboration, and we pride ourselves on our extensive range of partners, which include NGOs, businesses, governments and law enforcement. Through collaboration and sharing information with partners, we are building a global picture of MSHT. This global picture shows hotspots and trends of MSHT and allow us to extract meaningful insights that we then use to target our action, in order to prevent people being trafficked in communities around the world. MSHT is a global business that takes $150 billion in profit each year and affects over 40 million people worldwide. To sustain its business, MSHT needs to recruit a minimum of 8 million people a year to maintain its profitability and meet and increase the demand. STT understands that this errant economy can only be effectively disrupted by undermining these three business drivers. This is how we do that: * Recruitment ? STOP THE TRAFFIK uses digital platforms and social media to geo-target people and communities at risk, many of whom may be difficult to reach through traditional methods. Our campaigns raise awareness, share information, and change behaviour related to MSHT. * Money - STOP THE TRAFFIK works with banks and other financial services organisations to understand how MSHT transactions can be identified, defining typologies and specific indicators. * Demand ? Businesses demand cheap workforce, services and products, meaning they face MSHT risk in their operations, supply chains, and to their customers. STOP THE TRAFFIK provides businesses with intelligence-led support to manage and prevent these risks. Due to Covid-19, almost all our work with businesses was put on hold as their operations changed. This, and a decline in individual giving experienced by the sector, meant that our funding for this financial year is down 10% (approximately £60k). However, Covid-19 has not only affected our business clients and donors. Covid-19 has exacerbated the risk to people of, or in, exploitation. Our intelligence has confirmed this, providing additional key insights into the specific groups at increased risk of exploitation and how traffickers are evolving to take advantage of their vulnerabilities. Therefore, we have diverted our focus to the delivery of our community campaigns. These campaigns, which we plan, design and implement, are a vital response to an increased need for changes in awareness, knowledge and behaviour of people in or at risk of MSHT. We have not furloughed any staff or made any redundancies, rather diverted the focus of team members to work on campaigns. Still, our present team is now under extreme pressure to deliver an effective response to this urgent need. Ongoing STT community campaigns and trusted partnership work, combined with our growing incident database, is identifying targets for continuing our work. Intrinsic to the delivery of our community campaigns is the need for analysis, communication, MEL, partnership building and coordination. All of this is currently drawn from our team, which comes at a cost. In addition to this, by increasing our service delivery in response to Covid-19, there are increased costs related to their effective implementation and conclusion of this work. We are in a fragile funding environment, with uncertainty around previously guaranteed funding streams. The emergency fund from Comic Relief would enable STT to commit to the resilience required to increase our delivery. In addition to this, Covid-19 emergency funding from Comic Relief would also positively impact the wider community, including people of BAME origin, who our research has shown as being significantly more vulnerable to MSHT. Furthermore, our community campaigns also equip people who may know a vulnerable person in, or at risk, of exploitation with the information they need to signpost them to appropriate help and support.

data.title: Student MindsRecovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -One of our main priorities is to produce resources for students that will empower them to look after their own mental health and support those around them through the pandemic and the turbulent months and years to come. To understand their needs, we are conducting fortnightly surveys and have had numerous one to one conversations with university staff and students. Through this work, we have determined that students face a number of unique and complex problems during this time. Whilst there are numerous high-quality resources available covering general advice on looking after your mental health during lockdown, these do not offer support on coping with the issues solely faced by the student population that we have identified. These issues include uncertainty around academic assessment, moving out of halls to unsupportive living environments, and facing a turbulent graduate jobs market. We have identified a number of student groups who would benefit from even more specific resources. This includes international students who are either separated from relatives and experiencing racism and financial hardship (without recourse to benefits) in the UK, or are back home and accessing online teaching from an unsuited timezone. As the UK?s only student mental health charity, we alone have the expertise, insight and network of student and sector contacts required to create this tailored material. To reflect trends amongst Generation Z in preferential mediums for content consumption, the content we produce will be a mix of written content and video content. It will be co-produced with clinical professionals and students to ensure it is evidence-based, safe and relevant. We will disseminate this content through institutions and sector organisations such as UCAS to reach as many students as possible. 
 
 
 Over the next few months, we will also be adapting our current core workshops and training programmes to be delivered online and be relevant to the current context, for we have a duty to our beneficiaries to be agile and adaptive. Again we will work with volunteers and clinical professionals to ensure the materials are safe and meets beneficiaries? needs.
 
 This student-facing work will incur staffing costs for the analysis of survey responses, content creation and dissemination, and supervision of volunteers. We also require funding to pay external clinical reviewers for their support. There are other costs to moving to a digital focus, including software, external video editing, and website development. 
 
 Our sector-facing team have also shifted their focus. They are working with government departments, universities and students? unions, using the insight from our social listening and surveys to inform their strategies for supporting the mental health of university communities as they plan ahead for the upcoming academic year. An emergency grant would also help to fund the salaries of the staff members involved in this vital work with far-reaching influencing potential. 
 
 Finally, it is important that we keep our core structures in place to ensure the long-term sustainability of the charity. If one thing is clear, it is that this pandemic will have a profound impact on student experiences for a long time to come - and we are determined to be there to champion, influence and support positive mental health and wellbeing for as long as we are required.

data.title: Supporting professionals to detect and respond to economic abuse
data.description:
COVID19 -SEA has successfully developed and delivered a training programme for professionals working with victim-survivors of economic abuse. In light of social distancing measures, SEA is now seeking funding to reorient our training programme to online provision, so that it remains available and accessible to the community of professionals providing support for victim-survivors of economic abuse, responding to need and demand over the next 6 months. 
 
 SEA?s successful training programme comprises the following modules:
 - Understanding economic abuse in the context of domestic abuse;
 - Recognising the signs of economic abuse and the impact it has on victim-survivors;
 - Increased knowledge of forms of economic abuse during, on leaving and post-separation;
 - Understanding perpetrator tactics and the wider system challenges faced by victim-survivors;
 - Reflection on practice and identifying ways to improve responses.
 
 The programme includes OCN-accredited modules, and is aimed at a wide audience including professionals from domestic abuse charities, money/debt advice services, local authorities, the police, the housing sector, and the banking and insurance industry. 
 
 The requested funding will enable us to reorient this into an online training programme, for which we will seek OCN-accreditation. We envisage doing this by offering three linked options:
 
 E-learning package 
 The e-learning package will offer a starting point for learners, an introduction to economic abuse, and it may be done at any time to suit each participant. We envisage that many will realise the need to undertake the online training as a result. 
 
 Online workshops 
 Providing face to face training is an important means of engaging participants, offering an interactive process, facilitating networking, confirming participants? knowledge and understanding, and eliciting a commitment to change practice. The online workshops will aim to recreate this environment, hosted by an experienced facilitator. SEA is exploring available platforms with a range of functionality in order to do this. 
 
 Webinars 
 Webinars are an ideal way of focusing on a specific topic in more detail. SEA plans to develop a series of webinars to be made widely available to a larger and potentially more diverse audience. 
 
 The three components of the programme things will complement each other and be supported by the suite of specialist resources (Tools to Support) that are available for professionals via SEA?s website. SEA?s Tools to Thrive for victim-survivors will also support professionals? work, including four new resources we have developed in response to Covid-19.
 
 The increased reliance on online communications since the Covid-19 outbreak can be built on, and SEA will seek to maintain an online relationship with learners e.g. through regular newsletters, circulating links to updated resources, sharing news and success stories. We will also explore setting up an online forum for training participants to continue discussions and to share ideas and best practice informally. 
 
 The training will be publicised widely through existing partnerships and networks, and also via the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG), Local Government Association, the Association for the Directors of Social Services, Local Authority safeguarding leads and councils for voluntary services, domestic abuse local partnership boards. 
 
 The target audience will be any service provider with a new statutory duty placed on them by the Domestic Abuse Bill, as well as domestic abuse charities, advice services, etc. A recent evaluation of Economic Abuse Training delivered to police Domestic Abuse Matters champions by SEA in partnership with SafeLives suggested ?the training would benefit other statutory agencies with social workers and health professionals listed as separate examples.?
 
 The project will be delivered over 6 months. The first two months will focus on developing the training modules and gaining accreditation. The next step will be marketing the training programme and taking bookings. The final three months will focus on delivering the training and reviewing and refining the programme. 
 
 At this stage we envisage delivering the following outputs:
 - An e-learning package freely available online via a registration portal
 - 30 online training workshops (up to 10 participants in each)
 - Monthly webinars (6 in total) 
 
 The delivery model will be regularly reviewed in response to the evolving context, social distancing measures and analysis of risks.
 
 Until the Covid-19 outbreak, SEA was working on a business plan to develop the earned income potential of the training programme. In light of the current context, this has been temporarily put on hold. The requested grant will enable SEA to continue delivering vital training over the next 6 months. When social distancing measures are sufficiently eased, SEA will be in a strong position to transition back to delivering face to face training (whilst also retaining components of the online training offer) and develop the earned income stream to be self-sustaining long term.

data.title: Sutton Coldfield YMCA Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -Funding will be used to extend the reach of our ?Virtually Minded? Project, which will be adapted to engage YMCASC beneficiaries that sit outside of currently funded target group. 
 We will support 45 beneficiaries who attend other YMCASC services, but currently fall outside of Virtually Minded target range and that are in COVID-19 vulnerable groups, through a range of remotely delivered activities, which are intended to;
 - support beneficiaries with their mental health during the period of shielding and lockdown
 - help beneficiaries to connect with peers and be part of an online community
 - reduce isolation and loneliness.
 
 Activities will be delivered remotely using zoom, phone and video calls, text messages and social media platforms that include;
 - weekly virtual mental health and mindfulness group workshops via zoom
 - online interactive creative art workshops via zoom (either group sessions or one2one dependent on learning ability)
 - virtual campaigns to help people to address isolation and loneliness using social media (via Instagram, tick tock, Facebook etc)
 - one2one remote mental health life-coaching sessions via video or phone
 - a ?device? loaning scheme for those who cannot afford tech to enable them to connect with people online (a number of our beneficiaries fall within this category)
 Formats will be changed to reflect different ages and abilities; the use of creative media will feature prominently, forming the foundation for sessions & providing the key to enabling beneficiaries? to express/articulate their feelings & emotions. 
 To do this we need;
 - Extra staffing hours
 - Extra I-pads and apple pens (loaned out to enable participants to connect online and engage in online creative workshops
 - extra laptops for staff remote working (we do not currently have enough laptops for all staff)
 - Creative resources packs (to be distributed to beneficiaries)
 - Travel (delivery of packs)
 - Extra overheads and management costs
 - PPE (for delivery of packs)
 - Zoom membership (2 accounts)

data.title: Tender Education and Arts Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 -In 2019, Tender was awarded a Tech vs. Abuse grant from Comic Relief to develop the concept for an online game that will support young people with SEND* to practice healthy relationships, recognise the warning signs of abuse and learn how to access support. *SEND refers to special educational needs and disabilities. Once complete, this resource will enable Tender to support hundreds of vulnerable children to be protected from abuse and access vital education and social skills. We are seeking funding to bring it to completion, tailor our delivery during social distancing, and eventually make it available for schools and caregivers. Teenagers with SEND face numerous challenges in forming relationships and are twice as likely to experience abuse as their non-disabled peers. This is exacerbated by a severe lack of accessible resources that support them to recognise abuse and develop healthy relationships. Removed from their usual support and peer networks during Covid-19, these young people are particularly isolated, and, in many cases, unable to identify or seek support for abuse if it is happening to them. Prior to Covid-19 measures, we worked in partnership with a digital agency and specialist schools to develop the concept and learning outcomes for this resource. Our co-design sessions with young people have enabled us to create a full Game Design Document and a prototype of what gameplay could look like. This has been tested by young people, parents, teachers and gaming professionals, with positive results: ?I think playing this game would help me get more confident trying to have a relationship in the real world? - Young person in a Tender user-testing session, Spring 2020 We are now seeking funding to: - Bring the complete resource to life through programming and scripting- Where possible, continue involving young people in the creative process: thus providing education, social development and boosts to their self-esteem during social distancing- Begin using the resource to support our delivery, and to support schools and caregivers.

data.title: Thames Reach Recovery Funding

data.title: The Positive Change Partnership
Recovery and Sustainability
data.description: COVID19 -The funding is requested to ensure Baobab?s recovery and sustainability following COVID-19. There are three areas of concern that we have, and we would like your help to address:- The pandemic has illustrated just how vital it is for a small charity like Baobab, to have in place a good, appropriate level of reserves. We currently hold the equivalent of around 4 months? running costs in reserves. We have built them up gradually and painstakingly over time. Without them, we would have been extremely vulnerable. We feel that the future of fundraising, particularly the area that we focus on ? fundraising from trusts, foundation and grant-makers ? will now be more competitive than ever due to increasing need demand from charities whose community fundraising income have disappeared practically overnight. Keeping our reserves steady is a priority for us going forward.- Because key staff have been redeployed, we haven?t been able to do as much fundraising as usual. Baobab only has one full-time member of staff; the rest are all part-time. The safety and well-being of the young people we support is our absolute priority, so our small team have in part been redeployed. For example, our Fundraising Administrator who would usually be applying for funding at present has been directly supporting the young people by organising and delivering food parcels and mobile phones. We are concerned fear that our income will be negatively affected as a result. We have a deficit of £112,000 We were feeling confident that the applications we have made over the past 4 months would be successful as they are to very long-term supporters. However, we are getting a strong message that whilst our work is still likely to be supported, it won?t be at the levels requested. So, for example, we had asked The Alan and Babette Sainsbury Fund for £15,000 p.a. and they have given us £5,000 p.a. And a recent conversation with The Roddick Foundation (to whom we have applied for £50,000) confirmed that they are going to focus on smaller grants. Currently only 60% of our deficit is covered and we are becoming increasingly concerned that the applications about which we were very confident ? pre COVID-19 - will be much reduced.Your funding would therefore help us to clear our deficit so that we do not need to use our reserves. It will ? assuming the other funding we are expecting to come in ? enable us to start our financial year without a deficit and therefore to be able to be in a position to weather future storms. With your help, we will be able to make good progress with fundraising and to get into a position where we can fare well in a highly competitive fundraising environment and be prepared for a possible prolonged period of fundraising in a recession.

data.title: The Booth Centre Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -Funding to enable The Booth Centre to re-open in a safe way so that we can provide face to face support to people who are homeless or at risk of homelessness. This would include running an advice service 9-12 Monday to Friday, an activities programme Monday to Friday mornings, a volunteering programme which enables people who come to the Booth Centre to work with us to run the service, co-production groups to help us to plan and evaluate our work and to work with the Council and other services to reshape homelessness services in the city. We also want to re-model our Job Club to enable us to operate more online/by phone and to expand it, so that we are able to help people to get into work and avoid financial and work force exploitation. COVID-19 has resulted in lots of car washes and other businesses which were trapping people in a trafficking situation to escape and we would like to help them to get work and secure accommodation.- To do this we need to have: 
 - A full time cleaner who will clean toilets after each person has used them and clean other areas of the Centre on a continual basis.
 - A member of staff welcoming people to the Centre, ensuring people, who need to wait outside before they enter, are socially distancing; ensuring that people are using hand sanitiser when they enter the building and explaining the social distancing arrangements. 
 - Additional consumables ? cleaning materials, PPE for staff and volunteers, hand sanitiser and masks for everyone, take away food containers ? as not everyone will be able to eat in the Centre
 - Phones to enable us to run a virtual job club to back up and expand our face to face job club and enable people who are at risk of workplace exploitation to get legal work ? we would want to provide 100 people with smart phones with some data/credit.
 We have the challenge of moving from an open door service for homeless people, which historically was used by 80 ? 100 individuals a day to a service which is still open and welcoming and encourages a social atmosphere which is good for people?s mental health and allows us to build relationships with some of the most excluded individuals but also ensures safe social distancing. We want to ensure our adapted service is delivered within our values to being Inclusive and welcoming.

data.title: The British Institute of Human Rights ecovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -We are requesting funding to assist us to support people in vulnerable situations and their community groups to be able to use human rights advocacy to ensure public officials and decision-makers are accountable for decisions that impact their lives during Covid-19. We need support to help us transform our delivery to more digital and online channels, rather than our more usual face-to-face sessions and support. Our theory of change is that when people are supported to translate human rights law into a practical advocacy tool this leads to significant local change that can address and prevent everyday social injustices. In our model people are not vulnerable, but have been put in vulnerable situations. Framing social justice issues as human rights issues empowers people to move beyond asking for charity or goodwill, to calling on powerful bodies to comply with the law. We work directly with people and their community groups to empower them to make change using human rights advocacy. Covid-19 has significantly impacted our working model; we have had to adapt and learn quickly, and we are therefore seeking funding which will enable BIHR to support people by:
 
 1) Translating the huge complexity of changes to law and policy as a result of Covid-19 into easy to understand language, enabling people to navigate what this means for their lives. In particular people with care and support needs face huge risks with sweeping changes to the law that allow previous legal duties to provide support (such as washing and dressing) to be suspended. This is alongside removal of duties to allow people to have choices about support, the requirement for assessments or reviews, and the removal of duties around children's special educational needs. The Coronavirus Act is law for 2 years (with very limited options for 6-monthly reviews). The legacy of these will be significant, and beyond the immediate public health issues of the pandemic. Therefore, we need the resourcing now to enable us to put in place the systems for this vital analysis and dissemination for now, to deliver further benefits over the coming 18 months. 
 
 2) The only proviso to the Coronavirus Act changes is that they cannot breach people's legally protected human rights. Clearly, people must be able to raise their human rights with decision makers (e.g. social workers, housing and care providers, etc.). We therefore need to shift our community support sessions which people this knowledge and confidence to online sessions. We have been able to pilot 2 sessions with people, demonstrating the impact we can enable. Before our session 100% of people were worried about the impact of Covid-19 on their human rights (life, liberty, family life, being discriminated against), yet the average confidence level of raising this with officials was 2.4/5. After our sessions this rose to 4.3/5, with over 70% of people able to challenge decisions about their care and support of those of someone they care for. As one disabled person feedback in our evaluation: "Really worth taking part. So often feels decisions are made about me without me and I had no idea what my rights were. I feel empowered now to start to know how to go about making sure mine and other disabled people in similar situations can look at our rights being upheld." We know the demand for this support is huge, and self-led organisations across the country want to work together with us to provide these sessions to their members, co-producing what people need to protect themselves. 
 
 3) Bolster and embed our community support sessions with free accessible sharable online resources on people?s human rights during Covid-19 (and for the 2-year period from March, as this is how long the legal changes last, review is very limited and only every 6 months). These will map our community sessions, above, which we plan to develop around the general issues of people?s human rights and care and support law changes, and specific issues. These include the right to life as many disabled adults are worried about having do no resuscitate orders placed on their medical files, as are parents of disabled children. Family life rights are also being consistently raising with us, ensuring family contact is supported in creative ways and not simply stopped leaving vulnerable adults and children alone and their mental health compromised. We are planning for further themed resources developed with people themselves.
 
 4) Support a communities of practice approach with the people and groups we work with, so that their voices can be heard in the reviews and inquiries into the government?s handling of Covid-19. Already there are 3 UK parliamentary inquiries, and 2 Scottish assembly inquiries. These reviews are important, but too often the voices of the people affected are missing. We believe our work will directly reach 1000 people. This provides a huge and unique opportunity to work with people to develop a community of practice model that enables those we are supporting to be heard and influence the calls for accountability.

data.title: Faw Cett Society Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 -We are seeking funding to support our #MakeWomenVisible campaign and coalition response to the COVID crisis. The funding would provide a contribution towards 6 months? salary costs for our campaigns and communications team who are delivering this reactive campaign. Since March we have rapidly grown a coalition of over 80 women?s organisations and have co-ordinated an immediate joint statement and combined calls to action. Alongside this, we are publishing our own surveys to evidence the impact on women and girls. Our work is divided in to three phases. Phase one is the immediate crisis response (March ? May). Phase two is exiting the lockdown which is the phase we are currently in (May onwards) and which may run for some months depending on whether or not we experience a second peak of the virus. Phase three is the programme for renewal. The preparation for this phase needs to begin now as we mobilise our coalition to develop an agenda to try to influence how we emerge from this crisis. There is a significant risk that we could see progress on gender equality reversed by this crisis and policy decisions made which could impose another wave of austerity which we know hits women (low paid, BAME) hardest. To do this effectively requires a significant input of staff time and resource across a number of functions in the team (policy, campaigns and communications). An additional £35k in the next 6 months would help to fill an emerging gap in our funding. The COVID-19 pandemic is likely to have a profound and lasting impact on the way we live our lives, and a negative impact on gender equality. Yet we can see that women are absent from decision-making as tens of billions of pounds of public money is being spent. There has been no published UK government gender impact or equality analysis, no recognition of the very different impact the virus and the policy and public spending response will have on women?s and men?s lives. This would benefit both women and men as initial data suggest that men are more likely to die from COVID-19. Yet we see that women are particularly on the frontline as they are the ones who are most likely to be providing health and social care services or doing unpaid caring for loved ones. The impact of school and nursery closures will have a significant impact on women?s ability to do paid work, with women more likely than men to take on the unpaid care of children. They are likely to reduce their working hours or lose their jobs as a result. We also know that workers in the bottom-five broad occupational groups are extremely unlikely to be able to work from home. Research shows that these occupations account for 42 per cent of people in employment. Women are the majority of those living on the lowest incomes and in insecure work, eg Women hold 70% of jobs not entitled to Statutory Sick Pay. They are also more likely to be dependent on social security system and Universal Credit, living in temporary accommodation or poor quality housing.Women are the majority of workers in shutdown sectors. To date, the majority of those who have lost their jobs in this crisis are women. Evidence also suggests that the gender pay gap will grow as a result of the crisis as women are reporting larger falls in pay than men. The unequal impact of caring roles during this crisis is also likely to contribute to a widening of the gender pay gap.

data.title: Magdalene Trauma Informed Practitioner
data.description: COVID19 -We would like to request additional funding for the following. Additional management support in both our young people?s and women?s teams, reflecting a considerable increase in need, and back office and senior management support essential to maintaining project delivery. The Doorway women?s service workload has doubled in the weeks following 23rd March 2020. Not only are they seeing an increase in the number of women with complex and multiple needs who are accessing the service, but the number and range of needs each individual woman is seeking support for and the amount of crisis situations has intensified. The women we work with do not engage with other services and the Doorway team have worked steadily over the years to build trusted relationships, therefore we are well placed to get them in touch with the voluntary and statutory services they require support from to ensure their individual safety and decrease risk to public health given the complex and multiple needs they experience often resulting in risk taking and chaotic behaviour. This work is now further compounded as face-to-face visits are no longer taking place, contacts, and multi-agency meetings are being completed remotely and we are being asked to represent our vulnerable woman in many areas such as probation, housing, domestic violence, adult social care and many others. For Rose young people?s service demand from the young people already accessing the service has increased by 55%, whilst referrals remain steady, in the weeks following 23rd March 2020. Our Rose team is deemed essential by the local authority and has continued to complete face-to-face visits with the most at risk young people throughout this period. In addition to this it has been documented nationally that young people are struggling with the lockdown, as well as being at increased risk of online exploitation and abuse. A rise in referrals reflecting this is expected in the coming weeks. We have moved to remote working which has seen an increase in need for our IT support, this has been reflected in invoices post 23rd March 2020. Additional funds will be required to cover these costs. Our Projects Administrator is currently continuing to develop our online, digital, and communications offer which is more important now than ever. We expect this work to form the backbone of our adaptability and therefore sustainability in continuing to provide effective and efficient services in the coming 6 months. Looking ahead to the coming months we are preparing to return to the workplace, in measured and appropriate steps. It has been noted by our frontline practitioners in both our women?s and young people?s services that it is difficult for them to separate work and home life, beyond what one would normally expect. This is due to the type of work they are doing, working daily with women?s and young people?s trauma. Trauma can be linked to space, place and time and therefore when frontline practitioners are supporting someone with trauma in their own home it can mean that secondary trauma is brought into their personal, usually, safe spaces. As a result of this staff have been encouraged to engage with our independent clinical supervisor more frequently and management support has been increased where needed to ensure our staff are appropriately safeguarded. We are also looking at taking on additional office space to enable frontline staff to return to office space safely. This will ensure that team cohorts (one of which is still having face-to-face sessions with young people) do not mix and to allow for social distancing to be observed effectively. Furthermore, when we do move into the next stage of lockdown easing it is likely we will look to start face-to-face contact with our women. We know that for the women we work with getting Covid-19 would have devastating effects due to their complex and multiple needs and therefore creating team and service ?bubbles? would allow for this to happen safely. Additional funds to ensure safety of staff, women, young people and their families will be required in the next 6 months in order to allow services to continue to provide the support urgently needed. The work volume has increased for managers (team and senior), support staff and contractors, who are constantly supporting frontline staff with safeguarding concerns as well as monitoring, reviewing, and adjusting best practice to keep staff, clients, young people and their families safe across the two teams. To enable us to continue to respond to the developing demands on our services we will require additional resources over the next 6 months.

data.title: Venture TrustRecovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -We are seeking this funding to help with the recovery of our support services following lockdown. In response to the current crisis, we are delivering an online digital service ?Be Well, Be Connected, Be Ready? (See Q2.3). We have managed to secure funding to meet the new costs of this delivery until June, but there continues to be a financial risk to meeting the costs of our overheads and delivery staff during the ongoing recovery period.
 We have already seen a huge uptake of our online offer (see Q2.3), and we anticipate that following lockdown, our outdoor therapeutic approach will be more valuable than ever to help support the wellbeing of those struggling in Scotland. Based on Government advice and our own scenario forecasting, we are planning for a significant transition period before we can safely return to a 3-phase wilderness delivery model. This funding would help fund our staff salaries during this transition. 
 During this period, we are looking to move our wilderness services into communities, offering both 1-to-1 and carefully managed groupwork in local parks and greenspaces. Continuing our personal development approach, we would use low risk activities such as bush-crafts and local walks as conduits to introduce personal development concepts such as establishing trust/safe spaces; responsibility/accountability; emotion management; goal setting; confidence and resilience building and giving/receiving feedback. When safe to do so, we would then introduce daytrips slightly further afield, with abseiling, kayaking and longer hikes possible. Every activity would be front-loaded with discussion about skills individuals hope to develop, and interspersed with discussions where the group are coached to reflect upon what they have learnt and how this can be applied at home. 
 
 For those with more acute mental health issues, we also intend to offer a new personalised counselling service, utilising local outdoor spaces including parks, community gardens, woodlands or hills as tools for reflection and expression. Sessions will include elements of ?walk and talk? counselling, allowing a client to journey and be supported to explore/reflect on their internal and external landscapes. Sessions will also encourage clients to engage with natural materials and features as an expressive conduit, both verbally and non-verbally. For example, drawing shapes in the sand to represent internal experience or ?this fallen tree represents how I feel right now because??. This works as a means for the counsellor to interpret what the client is feeling, and direct reflective conversation. Currently, our trained therapists are working online (see Q2.3) with participants suffering with new or pre-existing anxiety, PTSD and other mental health issues. We are reaching capacity already, and so keen to continue this support when lockdown restrictions lift. 
 
 Ongoing, we intend to take the learning from both our digital and community-based approaches, and integrate these into our 3-phase offer, enabling us to work with participants for whom an extended residential may not be effective or viable.
 
 Funding from Comic Relief would help us to keep our essential delivery staff working and not furloughed, enabling us to continue to support participants safely and effectively during this challenging time, whilst also planning for a return to normal services.

data.title: Vineyard Compassion Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -1. Providing stability for the charity by funding core costs and overheads. This would allow us to continue existing work and adjust to changing needs. Core costs are difficult to fund as most grants at the moment are for emergency response. Our social enterprise income stopped overnight, which usually covered these core costs and overheads. Therefore, Comic Relief extra funding would help provide stability and help us to avoid depleting our reserves.
 
 2. Support an emergency response to an unmet need through the purchase of a mobile "Emergency Provisions" vehicle that could extend our crisis provisions support into the surrounding rural areas where we have seen evidence of increased need and a lack of accessibility to support. With reduced movement and social distancing, there are significant barriers to engagement. A mobile service would make this help more accessible. We propose to purchase an ex-library van/vehicle that would allow us to travel to various rural locations. We would provide "Emergency Provision Sessions" in a car park or discrete public space. The van would transport food/toiletries/household essentials and when restrictions safely permit give us space and the facility to bring clients on board to engage relationally. As we currently do in the Hope Centre we would provide one-to-one support through a needs assessment and support plan so we can meet their crisis needs and empower them to tackle the underlying root issues of poverty. While social distancing restrictions apply, we would have a weather proof canopy where clients can access provisions safely from the door/entrance to eliminate any contact. Over time we would hope to begin partnerships with other organisations who operate rurally, and collaborate together to offer this mobile service for their clients at their premises, thus extending our reach and supporting the effectiveness and impact of other organisations.

data.description:
COVID19 -We are receiving an increased amount of calls for support for older women experiencing domestic abuse.
 This together with staff showing symptoms of Covid-19 (one member of staff is currently self isolating with symptoms which means our ability to deliver a service is halved). The funding would cover costs for a frontline support worker and relevant administration costs. We also require funding to cover costs for those unable to access benefits, access through Wifi and to have a desktop computer in both refuges. Some extra funding for travel by taxi to enable access to our safe houses as the trains and buses in Wales are still not working. We are also having to pay for deep cleaning and the costs of replacements for bedding as we are unable as in the past to rely on our donations of bedding due to the restrictions so require funds for this.

data.title: Who Cares? Scotland Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -Care Experienced people already face disadvantage in their life, the Covid-19 pandemic has amplified this. From issues with homelessness to zero hour contracts and increased living costs, Care Experienced people are facing the hardest times of their lives alone without support. 
 We will provide a National Helpline, Information and Support service for Care Experienced people facing crisis. We have provided a National Helpline service since March offering support financially, as well as practically but as the situation evolves, so does the needs of Care Experienced people. Many children and young people may find support with Advocates, Social Work and throughcare workers. 
 Adults who are termed 'Care-Leavers' are often left lacking the support throughout these challenging times, they don't have the networks, family and connections to ask for help. Many have poor mental health, they struggle to manage their personal finances, they don't have anyone to help them apply for benefits or support, someone talk to organisations on their behalf, they aren't aware of their rights - essentially they need someone to listen and help them through difficult circumstances. This is what the National Helpline, Information and Support Service will achieve.
 This funding will contribute towards the cost of our evolving National Helpline service with Manager salary and associated costs.

data.title: WILD Recovery Funding
data.description:
COVID19 -We would like to request funding to enable us to sustain and further develop our remote offer, to meet the increased need (both in terms of number of families and complexity of need). This would include:
 - Capacity to maintain and develop our current, much expanded, Comms offer ? across facebook, Instagram, youtube and twitter . A worker would coordinate our Comms, develop video and visual content, and support young parents to be involved in Comms (such as our recent social media takeover week). They would also lead the development of our cybersafety, using the CR-funded AVA/CAST resource pack.
 - Training and development hours for children?s work team members to develop an online ?Attachment? programme. We have spent the last few weeks firefighting, where the bulk of support has been crisis intervention. We don?t want to lose our vision of intergenerational change, and want to find a way to support parents to build attachment and early language skills while working remotely, producing content which parents can use on a daily basis.
 - Evaluation support to properly evaluate our new ways of working, so that we can carry forward the best practice into our future offer post-c19
 - SMT backfill to enable a stronger focus on financial stability over the next two years ? helping us move forward from a current ?pause? in some of our planned future funding.

data.title: Winner Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 -We would like to extend our offer of support around escaping and surviving domestic abuse to women who have no recourse to public funds. We will employ a worker for 30 hours per week to concentrate on supporting 15 women over six months to enable them to escape, access safe housing and begin the process of getting leave to remain. We will work intensively with these women to ensure that they can overcome the significant barriers associated with uncertain immigration status, communication and language difficulties and responsibilities for dependents. Through our sister organisation, Hull Women's Network, which is based in our centre, we will be able to source appropriate safe accommodation for them and any children they may have to begin the process of supporting them to recover from the trauma they have suffered. The support worker will be able to spend dedicated time with each woman to enable her to navigate the complex process of accessing the Domestic Violence concession and subsequently relevant benefits. Hull Women's Network will bank roll the rental payments until the housing benefit claim is approved and backdated. In this way we will be able to address the needs of a very vulnerable client group whose risk has been significantly exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic

data.title: Promoting the Rights of Scots to Live Well and in Dignity
data.description: COVID19 -We are requesting funding to support us with a digital inclusion support project to reduce barriers in to our community members in engaging with the digital world. Digital poverty/literacy has always been a barrier for our community members, but under the current lockdown measures this has seriously increased, leaving many asylum seekers socially isolated with no means of communicating and engaging with friends, family or crisis response services which are in operation. Most of the individuals we support have traditionally relied on public sources of wifi and access to telephones such as attending our drop ins, using public wifi available in community centres, libraries and public transport etc and are now no longer able to do so. Whilst ourselves and other services have responded quickly to put services online to reduce social isolation and provide sources of information, many of the individuals we support do not own or have access to any devices to enable them to get online, either not having a smartphone which can support the apps required, or not having the financial means to afford phone credit/data. We have managed to secure some emergency funding to purchase a limited number of devices/data top ups to start up a digital lending scheme to support those who are still digitally excluded but we are aware that lack of devices is only part of the problem, and with many language and literacy barriers further support is required to ensure that individuals understand how to use the devices, the apps required for accessing activities and how to keep themselves safe online. We are also now aware that this need will continue longer than first anticipated creating a greater demand for this support. We also want to ensure that devices are managed responsibly, protecting everyone?s privacy and that we have an adequate resource for ensuring devices are wiped properly before being redistributed to other users. We are aware through network discussions with our colleagues in other smaller integration networks in Glasgow that there is a wide need for this support but our colleagues have limited capacity to support a lending scheme, or do not do direct service delivery, so we would like to increase the number of devices we are able to distribute to facilitate taking referrals from our partners across the city for those they identify as in need of this service. We are therefore asking for funding support to develop a more cohesive digital inclusion service. We would like to purchase additional devices for a referral scheme which has a reach beyond our own community members to asylum seekers being supported through some of our partners in the city. To ensure this is managed appropriately we would plan to employ a digital inclusion assistant who will take responsibilty for managing the devices, using a purchased device management software system, and provide support to those receiving the devices to ensure they are able to understand how to use these . The digital inclusion worker will also work closely with our in house interpreting service and social media volunteers to ensure that all our social media platforms including our website are providing up to date information on Covid 19 and how to access support in multiple languages. The worker will also develop a training pack to train up members of the asylum community as digital champions so that moving forward, they can develop their own digital skills to a level that they are then able to provide support to their peers in getting online and engaging with online activities. This training will be devised in different languages, based on the Digital Champion pack produced by SCVO which is currently being trialled in Govan as part of the Scottish Government?s Connected Scotland pilot scheme.

data.title: Grenfell Urgent Action
data.description: BA Flying Start for Grenfell - Oxford Gardens is one of the key local primary schools and they have been deeply affected by the fire. Whilst not one of the schools directly damaged (so have not received much additional funding) they have families who lived in the tower and surrounding walkways who are now displaced and have sadly lost pupils, friends and family members. The school has developed a plan to support pupils over the next year and have received a small amount of funding from Government (DCLG) and Tudor Trust for a support worker to come into the school. Our funding is proposed to cover a week long residential for their year 6 pupils (disproportionately affected and also in a difficult transition year) and arts therapy for all pupils. The residential is particularly important they feel to provide respite away from the physical reminders of their trauma and space for them to reflect. And really importantly to allow the children to have some fun and have something to look forward to. Whilst we do not usually fund schools we are able to fund them, and in this instance it makes sense to support an organisation working with the children on a daily basis.

We were able to source some from Digital Leeds but they have now run out of equipment.- Additional temporary management salary costs to allow us to both re-start and re-engineer the service and focus on medium and long term strategy and sustainability. - Salaries for front-line staff and management to establish a telephone support/drop-in offer for those women who need limited initial support and/or support to access other services.- Plastic screens and additional cleaning resources to enable us to re-start work at Portland Street, our Leeds city-centre premises.- PPE and taxi costs for staff when we re-start working in the community. We are currently planning to use our reserves to cover these costs, however our reserves are not yet at recommended levels and this would increase the gap between actual and target reserves. Our 2018/19 accounts showed reserves at £100,614 against a target of £143,000. Our 2019/20 accounts are being finalised but we don?t expect reserves to have significantly increased.

data.title: Art therapy & integrated support for young people in Hackney struggling with mental ill-health
data.description: Currently 10% of young people in the UK are thought to have a diagnosable mental health disorder. In Hackney, risk factors for mental ill-health including family violence, homelessness, unemployment, substance abuse and gang violence are all higher than the national average. In response to this, Off Centre provides counselling, therapy, information and advice, and mentoring to young people in Hackney who have mental health needs. As part of this service, Comic Relief will fund their art therapy work, including one-to-one and group sessions. The therapy supports young people to understand themselves better, become more confident and resilient, and improve their mental health and wellbeing.

data.title: Yorkshire MESMAC Recovery Funding
data.description: COVID19 -We are seeking to address the increased isolation brought on by the lockdown measures and the social distancing guidance currently in place. Our most vulnerable service users (People living with HIV, BAME, older people LGBTQ+) are unable to take advantage of online spaces to help ease the effects of isolation either due to lack of funds or lack of skills in technology and software. This increased isolation impacts mental health, general wellbeing and service users? resilience in what are already challenging times. We have trialed a small run of this project to evidence the need and effectiveness. The funding will provide: - An increase in current LGBTQ+ counselling provision by 300 sessions (50 new service users) - Tablets and data packages for 6 months to those service users without the means to be connected in a virtual space (people living with HIV, BAME, older LGBTQ+ people) - To provide training and support for people to make use of online support groups, video calling and how to stay safe in an online environment.
